Some observations:

* generally, at different levels of noise the models are still able to react to the increase and decrease in vmax. Obviously, the model does a better job at lower AR-noise and touristic bias
* adding more AR-noise can or cannot “bias” the relation between the true_vmax and the estimate. It seems that if relation is biased without AR-noise, adding AR-noise will spoil it even more. At the same time, it definitely seems to create more variance (but there’s no system in how the model over/underestimates the results)
* adding tourists seems to have a biasing effect on the model (i.e. the model consistently over/underreporsts the results)
* this seems to be clear – AR noise always creates “waves“ in different places, while touristic bias creates spurious correlation in one specific place (where it most probably correlates to some specific channel)

h1. Call with Kaufland 03.06.2025

Kaufland wants Bolt to be a Processor for loyalty card number



*Prepared Arguments*

# I reviewed the agreement Kaufland sent to Bolt (Individual contract for data processing by proxy) – it’s not fit for the arrangement between Bolt (a platform providing marketplace and IT services) and Kaufland (Store). Bolt is not a “supplier” of delivery services where data would flow from Kaufland (of Kaufland customers only) to Bolt. I saw Kaufland’s General Terms and they are not fit for this set up – more of a standard for manufacturer or supplier.



# Bolt cannot accept role as Processor as this does not fit our operation set up. 

* Bolt and Restaurant are separate data controllers: both determine their own means and purposes of processing. Bolt processes User’s personal data to offer marketplace and IT services, Kaufland processes Client’s personal data to fulfill sales agreement. These are different purposes for processing.
* Bolt decides on the main functionalities and data processing possibilities of our services (online platform). Kaufland has decided to use Bolt in aiding to connect them with their customers.
* Bolt is a controller when providing its relevant IT services, Kaufland is controller while using Bolt services when offering their goods. Bolt does not process perosnal data on behalf of Kaufland, Kafuland does not process personal data on behalf of Bolt.
* EDBP example: A travel agency is considered separate controller from airline and hotel service provider even if the travel agency sends personal data of its customers to the airline and a hotel, for making reservations for a travel package and the service providers confirm reservations. Each of the parties processes the data for carrying out their own activities and using their own means. In this case, all three service providers are separate controllers, processing the data for their own and separate purposes - _just as Bolt and Kaufland are processing data for their own purposes._



# Loyalty card number situation

* What is the reason why you want Bolt to be a processor of loyalty card number?
* Information is not of “sensitive nature” – low risk in cases of personal data breaches, etc. 
* Low risk of regulatory inquiries or scrutiny as well.
* Bolt has robust security measures in place, ISO certified, etc.
* Does Kaufland have any worries? I.e. potential misuse, etc. - to figure out how to address this
* Users enter this number to our platform – we take care of the security of processing, allow users to exercise their rights
* Operationally, as processor, we’d have to forward all data subject requests. Now, we receive thousands. We have automated export tool – we’d have to forward all requests to Kaufland.
* Bolt never acts as Processor – we have thousands of suppliers – mapping out our list of sub-processors would take months.

*Another update on this topic:*

Looks like we are going to be going live with e-bikes in London in August. There are three insurance topics, two of which should be easy(ish), but the third one is a business decision which involves this topic. 



* *Mandatory Insurances:*

Public, Products and Employers' Liability is already in place and sorted

* *Warehouse Insurances:*

This is currently being worked through, and there is a possible partnership with Dott/Tier

* *Non-Mandatory Insurances:*

This is the issue topic. 

Unlike some parts of Europe, the UK does not mandate that e-bikes need insurance. e-Scooters, yes; but bikes no. 

We currently have Personal Accident (PA) and Rider General Liability (RGL) insurance for European users. However, following Brexit, we need to be an insurer, broker, or agent to offer this type of insurance in the UK, even if we are not directly charging for it. (see notes and comments previously supplied on this ticket) 

Our UK broker has agreed to allow us to be an Appointed Representative (AR)of theirs, if we want to offer this insurance. They will cover all the cost, as we will buy the insurance from them, and they will earn a commission to cover the cost etc. They have also suggested that once costs are covered, as we will be an AR, they can also share some of the commission back to us 

However, becoming an AR of theirs will require some legal input. The UK directors of Bolt will need to be listed with the FCA, and unless there is someone else with a proven and demonstrated knowledge of insurance, I will also need to be noted as the ‘_Approved Person_’ with the FCA and [broker.|http://broker.In]

[In|http://broker.In] theory, nothing is stopping us from launching without this PA or RGL insurance, but this insurance acts as a claims and legal function for us. So, without insurance and their claims team, all incidents of a user injuring themselves or someone else or damaging someone’s property will come to the legal function to deal [with.|http://with.At]

[At|http://with.At] this stage, I can’t give you a number, as I’m not sure if the UK will be more like Germany, which has ~700 claims in a year or more like Slovenia, which has zero claims. On top of the insurance, dealing with the claims is also the first line of defence for us if something happens. i.e., a death or accident resulting in a severe disability [occurs. It|http://occurs.It] is also worth noting that I think only Lime buys PA and RGL, and all the other providers do not.

Therefore, this is an issue being raised because, without being an AR, we can’t offer insurance, and without insurance, all incidents will need to be dealt with by someone (assuming in legal); therefore, additional resources might be needed.

*Summary: Review of Lattice AI “Writing Assist” Terms*

# *What the tool is and what it introduces*

* _Writing Assist_ is an AI-powered feature in Lattice that helps improve written employee content such as reviews, feedback, and updates.
* It uses OpenAI’s language models to make text more inclusive, concise, and actionable.
* The feature processes employee-generated text (Input) and returns AI-generated suggestions (Output).
* The functionality introduces a new data flow where Input is shared with a third-party AI provider (OpenAI), although Lattice commits that the data is not used for model training.
* Use of the feature is optional.

# *Key concerns*

* *Unilateral change clause*: Lattice can change the terms of the AI Addendum at its sole discretion (Section 5), and continued use is considered acceptance of those changes.

Clause 5: “_At its sole discretion, Lattice may modify or replace any of the terms of this AI Addendum. Customer’s continued use of Lattice AI following any changes to the Lattice AI Addendum, once posted to Lattice’s website or otherwise communicated to Customer, constitutes acceptance of those changes._*”*

* *Liability disclaimer*: Lattice disclaims all warranties related to Output, including accuracy, bias, or fitness for purpose. The burden rests entirely on the customer.

Clause 8: “_Customer agrees that Lattice is not liable for any claims arising from any information, output, or advice provided by Lattice in connection with Lattice AI.”_

* *Prepare a DSA Addendum:*
** Add OpenAI as a named sub-processor; and

I ran the model with [no change in supply and 50% increase in demand|https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1-XP5MUncZ-dWnWj_bbGI0oX5a3gdP4w3]. While it does now suggest some price increases, it’s still very limited, despite expected 90%+ utilisation. Looks like the model is not handling such extreme case very well (perhaps improved by S2O modelling). Hard to say how sensitive drivers are really and whether we’re underestimating. AR has deteriorated -20pp since Jan - so they are sensitive to something. 

I also ran the model with [default seasonality assumptions, but increased AR elasticity|https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1J3DJ3uDMigbea7ox73RD3dEi8ax0jt09]. It’s now a mix of price changes, but still biassing towards lowering prices. I have some doubts whether utilisation will go as high as the model predicts given the declining AR trend.

Finally, ran the model with [default seasonality assumptions, but both increased AR and OH elasticity|https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1zaIabnEBhp8m8vszrgGP0riT6arL6dO0]. Almost no change in recommendations compared to previous run. So, I think we should validate what’s a realistic utilisation level - I don’t think elasticity alone will explain it. Unlike Wix’s drag-and-drop, Strapi is a “headless” CMS. Wouldn’t it be better to suggest the following then?*“The lessee can carry out maintenance and repair at unofficial dealerships, subject to the compliance with manufacturer’s specifications and the use of original or equivalent-quality parts”*Reasoning:

* At first, the decision on whether warranty is maintained or not lies 100% with the manufacturer and its dealership. So in theory they can claim warranty is void for any reason.
* If Bolt disagrees with the decision, for example because it violates the MVBER, Bolt would need to dispute with the manufacturer/dealership. Only if the warranty is deemed valid after the dispute would Bolt be able to prove it didn’t breach the lease framework. If Bolt needs to go to court because of this, it could take years.
* Complying with manufacturer’s standards and using original or equivalent parts is more objective and easier to prove to the bank (e.g., via independent expert), even if the manufacturer/dealership claims that warranty is void.

The lease framework should still spell out the consequences of the breach by Bolt. (edited)

* Bolt B2G will resell these services to the contracting authorities.

Although the subcontracting agreement will be between Bolt B2G and the fleet, all payment flows will be managed by Bolt Ops. To facilitate this payments flow without requiring a financial license, we rely on the commercial agency exception, under which:

* The fleet appoints Bolt Ops as its commercial agent to negotiate transportation service agreements with Bolt B2G.
* Bolt Ops collects payments from Bolt B2G on behalf of the fleet and transfers the funds to the fleet.
* Since the fleet uses the Bolt platform to provide services, Bolt Ops will deduct a commission for platform usage from the payments collected from Bolt B2G.

Dear Hassan,

 

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *4 April 2025*.

After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. {noformat}from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL

def detect_and_replace_outliers(train_df, var, period=7, threshold=0.5, show_plot=True):
    """
    Detects and replaces outliers using STL decomposition (trend + seasonality).
    An observation is considered an outlier if the absolute residual exceeds threshold * (trend + seasonal).
    """

    df = train_df.copy()
    df['date_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date_date'])
    df = df.sort_values('date_date').set_index('date_date')

    # STL expects a numeric index
    ts = df[var]

    # Apply STL
    stl = STL(ts, period=period, robust=True)
    result = stl.fit()

    df['trend'] = result.trend
    df['seasonal'] = result.seasonal
    df['residual'] = result.resid
    df[f'expected_{var}'] = df['trend'] + df['seasonal']

    # Outlier detection: relative deviation from expected
    eps = 1e-8
    deviation = np.abs(df[var] - df[f'expected_{var}']) / (np.abs(df[f'expected_{var}']) + eps)
    df['is_outlier'] = deviation > threshold

    if show_plot:
        plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
        plt.plot(df.index, df[var], label='Actual')
        plt.plot(df.index, df[f'expected_{var}'], label='Expected', color='orange')
        plt.scatter(df.loc[df['is_outlier']].index, df.loc[df['is_outlier'], var], color='red', label='Outliers')
        plt.title(f'STL Outlier Detection for {var}')
        plt.xlabel('Date')
        plt.ylabel(var)
        plt.legend()
        plt.grid(True)
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()

    print(f"Number of outliers for {var}: {df['is_outlier'].sum()}")

    # Replace outliers with expected value
    df.loc[df['is_outlier'], var] = df.loc[df['is_outlier'], f'expected_{var}']
    
    if show_plot:
        plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
        plt.plot(df.index, df[f'{var}'], label='Actual', alpha=0.6)
        plt.plot(df.index, df[f'expected_{var}'], label='Expected', color='orange')
        plt.title(f'Removed outliers for {var}')
        plt.xlabel('Date')
        plt.ylabel(var)
        plt.legend()
        plt.grid(True)
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()
    
    # Drop extra columns
    df = df.drop(columns=['trend', 'seasonal', 'residual', f'expected_{var}', 'is_outlier'])

    return df.reset_index(){noformat}

* clearly communicate that participation is voluntary and not linked to any work obligations;
* make clear the gift card is a token of appreciation, not payment for services; Although the amount is modest, *gift cards may be considered income* under French tax law if they're tied to work performance or obligations. If authorities view the gift card as a *professional incentive*, it could trigger *social security contribution obligations* or *tax reporting* for Bolt or the recipient.


+*Recommendations for the communications*+*:*

* Use language that frames the gift card as a *thank-you for feedback* rather than a performance reward.
* Keep value modest (under €60-70 aligns with common thresholds).
* Consider issuing the gift card *outside the Bolt app* or usual payment infrastructure to reinforce its *non-compensatory nature*.
* Avoid repetition (i.e., don't regularly give gift cards to the same drivers).

Because you’re collecting opinions in a recorded interview (possibly with video), GDPR compliance applies. *I have created a subticket for the Privacy team to get pertinent safeguards re-this project and the contention of personal data in the survey questions.*


+*Conclusion & Green Light (with safeguards)*+*:*
You can proceed with the interviews and offer the €60 digital gift card, provided:

* participation is *voluntary and clearly optional;*
* the gift is *not framed as remuneration*
* you ensure *GDPR compliance (*+*checking this with Privacy*+*)*
* you *avoid recurring patterns* that suggest a regular reward scheme through surveys and interviews



*Short participation notice or consent blurb is suggested*, covering:

# *Voluntary nature* of participation

# *Nature of the gift* as a non-monetary thank-you

“If you’re selected for a short follow-up call, you’ll receive a €60 digital gift card as a token of appreciation for your time.”

+*Push Notification*+

*Clause 4.6 – Rent Reductions*

* May limit or exclude the tenant's statutory right to reduce rent under § 536 BGB.
* *Risk:* Bolt may be obligated to pay full rent even during material disruptions (e.g., insufficient power supply), unless established by a court.
* *Recommendation:* As a general rule, I would recommend pushing back on this point. However, since it's ultimately a commercial risk, I’ll leave the final decision to you.

*Clause 7.5 – Exclusion of Landlord's Strict Liability for Initial Defects*

* Excludes landlord’s liability under § 536a para. 1 alternative 1 BGB for defects existing at contract signing.
* *Risk:* Bolt bears the risk of pre-existing defects even without the landlord’s fault, including critical infrastructure issues.
* *Recommendation:* As a general rule, I would recommend pushing back on this point. However, since it's ultimately a commercial risk, I’ll leave the final decision to you.

*Clause 10.5 (old) / 10.7 (new) – Tenant’s Strict Liability for Structural Alterations*

* Tenant is liable for damages related to alterations, regardless of fault.
* *Risk:* Unreasonable liability exposure for Bolt, even for approved or necessary alterations.
* *Recommendation:* As a general rule, I would recommend pushing back on this point. However, since it's ultimately a commercial risk, I’ll leave the final decision to you. I applied some changes to at least exclude our liability for the LLs faults.

Hi [~accountid:712020:13ae7353-697f-46e7-99dd-8fc938931751],

Based on the analysis of Law No. 1333/98, which regulates the promotion of alcoholic beverages and tobacco, I do not identify any outright prohibition on the proposed campaign. However, please take the following into consideration when developing the marketing materials:

* *No Direct Promotion of Alcohol Consumption*
** You can co-brand with the beer company, but *must not encourage drinking* or suggest health/social benefits.
* *Mandatory Health Warning*
** All ads (digital, printed, etc.) must include this warning in *at least 10% of ad space*:
_“SU CONSUMO EN EXCESO DAÑA LA SALUD._
_ESTÁ PROHIBIDA SU VENTA A LOS MENORES DE 18 AÑOS._
_Lo advierte el Ministerio de Salud Pública y Bienestar Social.”_
* *Prohibited Content (Art. 8)*
** Avoid showing:
*** *Minors or characters appealing to minors*
*** *Family scenes* unless all participants are clearly adults
*** *Athletic or fitness-related activities*
*** *Sexual suggestions or imagery*
*** *Excessive or irresponsible consumption*
*** *Claims of health, social, or economic benefits*
* *Proximity Restrictions (although I do not think this will be relevant to us)*
** No advertising or tasting events *within 150 meters* of:
*** Schools
*** Health facilities
*** Government offices
* *Raffles, Contests, and Promotions (Art. 13)*
** You *cannot share the mechanics publicly*.
*** ❌ Not allowed:
**** “Buy X beer to enter the draw”
**** “Tag a friend to win”
**** “Spend Gs. 50,000 and get a raffle ticket”
*** ✅ Allowed:
**** “We’re running a special promotion. Visit the store for more details.”
**** “Ask your distributor how to participate.”
* *Promotional Materials Must Be Age-Appropriate*
** If possible ensure *online targeting tools* are used to restrict visibility to users over 18.
** *All participants and target audience must be 18+*
** Sampling or giveaways must be handled by staff *over 18* and given only to adults.



Additionally, I recommend raising a legal ticket for review once the marketing materials have been prepared.

If you have any questions in the meantime, please don’t hesitate to reach out.

Many thanks!

Hi [~accountid:61c02e8de7637900682fe2b2], thanks for your questions, you can find here below my feedback on both points: 

+*Conference for Drivers*+

Holding a conference to explain a new category to drivers is not inherently legally risky, _as long as it’s done correctly_ (participation is voluntary, meeting is informal, optional participation in the category, request consent if any personal data or feedback will be used…). 

*HOWEVER*, there are legal considerations to be addressed, such as reclassification and transparency. 

At this stage, I am not sure we have enough of a clear idea of how this category will be rolled out to hold a conference for drivers. 

* *With regards to the reclassification risk*: have we determined how we will ask the drivers to give the samples to the passengers only to those customers, what we will do if they offer rides when they no longer have samples, suspicion of fraud in keeping those samples… The way we decide how this category will work and how we interact with the drivers presents legal risks as this can be interpreted as an employer relationship of giving orders and monitoring their performance. 
* *Transparency*: in addition to the above, the practical aspects of the category are yet to be determined: how are the samples being collected, where to get them, when to opt in or opt out of the category, responsibility of Bolt or driver if no sample is available for passenger who paid the ride in this category… 

As long as we do not have a clear idea of how this category will be rolled out and we don’t have the answers to the questions the drivers may ask, I would not recommend holding a conference.

+*Category Description Proposals*+


I have reviewed the proposals and made some comments. As shared above, I think we still lack some information about how the category will work to confirm the most accurate description yet. 

As we continue to work on these descriptions, some general comments would be: 

* Not to include the word _“exclusive”_ (unless you have a legally exclusive agreement with a brand);
* Not to us the words “marques partenaires” (unless you have a signed agreement with a brand). 


If I am out of date with the developments and the new features of this category, happy to jump on a call to discuss this further ! 

Thank you !

[~accountid:5e5cb1623df51b0c93760cee] We are not counting the fraud rejected orders (cancelled orders) in this scenario. Fake order in Taiwan AML context is a ride that was not completed or was completed with signs of arrangement/manipulation. Best detection we have to cover these regulation determined scenarios it is RDNH detection: so three associated flags/detection we apply to the finished orders. So in AML regulatory context this is a ‘fake order’ scenario due to the coverage of certain regulatory points needing to reflect in our rules/detection. 

Inside the rule (data etc) ofc we can name this as we see fit to match the internal standards but on the rule context we need to refer to the fake orders in that sense.

Currently RDNH scenarios can happen from two ways in our detection/actioning: cases where we did the ‘revert order to rejected’ action and the scenarios where after the order we detect the order did not happen in it’s entirety like was predicted. In terms of Taiwan we need to cover the latter part - so cases where there was an actual order and later we determined it to be issue prone.

I’ve double-checked the first two scooters, and in both cases, the _collect_ task was created manually by an administrator. Regarding `CHARGER_REPORTED_PROBLEM` — we include the reason for opening if the _collect_ task is created immediately as a result of the report. In such cases, the `open_criteria` will contain: `..."criteria":"charger_report","comment":...`
However, if the _collect_ task was opened by a scheduled cron job, we don’t have detailed information about the underlying reasons. Adding that would require significant changes to the codebase. That’s why, in such cases, only a general marker is shown as the reason.

Since the supplier would be processing biometric data — which is considered a special category of personal data under the GDPR — we have reviewed their standard Data Processing Agreement (DPA) as part of the preliminary assessment.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
Based on this review, the DPA does not meet Bolt’s contractual standards in several critical areas. Key issues identified include:
{panel}

*Summary of key DPA issues*

# *We don’t get to approve their subcontractors (sub-processors)*🔴 
Synthesia reserves the right to bring in new vendors to process our data and only lets us know if we sign up for updates on their website. Our recommendation is to be able to formally approve any third parties they use, and get notifications to our privacy email without needing to log into their website.
# *No clear timeline for notifying us of a data breach*🔴
If there’s a security breach involving our data, we generally require notification within 24–48 hours. Their DPA doesn’t commit to any specific timing.
# *Our audit rights are limited and may come with costs*:orange_circle: 
Audit rights come with limitations on how Bolt can audit the partner and potentially chargeable costs. While limitation on audit rights are normal practice, we would ideally like to reduce the limitations suggested by the partner. This is medium risk.
# *Liability is vague and capped under their main contract*🔴
Liability is capped by reference to the master agreement and is expressed in the aggregate, which is not acceptable for high-risk processing (e.g. biometric data). There is also no standalone indemnity for data protection breaches, as usually required by Bolt. 
# *Security promises are only made via a website link*🔴
Synthesia references their security practices online (via a link), we need to lock those into the contract itself. Additionally, we need to include an additional clause to ensure that their security measures provide safeguards equivalent to those required under our [Infosec Code of Conduct|https://bolt.eu/en/security/supplier-requirements].

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Recommendation:* given these concerns and the sensitivity of the data involved, *if we decide to move forward with the supplier*, we recommend negotiating based on Bolt’s own DPA template to ensure appropriate contractual and regulatory protections are in place.

This will likely take a few weeks, if Synthesia is responsive.

Depending on the time sensitivity and your business priorities, we can also consider negotiating based on their template, but our recommendation is still to address the high risk issues we’ve flagged, especially the indemnity & liability bit.
{panel}



----

*On a separate note, I would like to confirm a few privacy compliance aspects with you regarding the project:*

# Could you please clarify how exactly we will provide the employee data to the Vendor? Does Bolt collect the photos of employees centrally, and then provides them to the Vendor?
# Once the Avatar has been created, what happens to the original data? Do you know if you will be able to delete this data from Synthesia without restrictions?
# In the event an employee wishes for their avatar to stop being used (e.g., employee termination), would it be possible to stop using their Avatar?

*Also, thank you for confirming that participation is voluntary. FYI:* because the creation of AI Avatars involves processing biometric data, we will need to obtain explicit consent from employees to participate.

# Used by non-employees (793.90):

* We need clarity on where data is hosted and whether any transfers outside the EEA occur. The DPA must include appropriate safeguards (e.g. SCCs, deletion rights, audit access).
* Assuming the DPA terms are acceptable and processing is limited to low-risk data, we do not see a blocker from privacy. However, this decision sits with the business, and the associated compliance overhead should be clearly owned locally.



Ultimately, we are happy for you to take a decision where commercially preferred, but please make sure the agreements are reviewed from your side, as Smartly will be liable for any data protection issues related to this agreement.

Hi [~accountid:712020:9c263122-6bc1-4bbe-91d7-c80d616c4514], it is mainly because fleets have no visibility into the driver block reasons or cashblock status unless informed by either the driver or Bolt directly.

When drivers are blocked, they are not able to take orders, and this means they don’t meet the fleet KPIs. 
Fleets need this information because the fleets are responsible for the driver’s performance, and they need that information to be able to decide whether to either:

# Support the driver to resolve the block or debt, or,
# Offboard the driver and reassign the vehicle in case it is a block that cannot be resolved.

		round(CAST(json_extract_scalar(opc."INPUT",'$.data.amount') AS double)*1.00/NULLIF(r.rate,0),2) AS payout_amount_eur,
		CAST(json_extract_scalar(opc."INPUT",'$.data.last_payout_timestamp')AS bigint) AS last_payout_timestamp,
		CAST(json_extract_scalar(opc."INPUT",'$.query.driver.payouts.last_payout_info.payout_id') AS bigint) AS last_payout_id,
		json_extract_scalar(opc."INPUT",'$.query.driver.payouts.last_payout_info.state') AS last_payout_state,

Provided input in relation to DSA reporting as follows:

*Disproportionate Data Collection Requirements:* Platforms are currently required to collect and report an extensive volume of granular data under the DSA. This includes the classification of illegal content into 17 high-level categories and over 60 sub-categories, with an obligation to enter data even where no content was flagged in a given category (e.g. reporting a value of “0” for non-applicable sub-categories).This produces *massive data redundancy* and requires technical solutions to simulate non-events, increasing operational costs without adding meaningful transparency.

This level of granularity not only requires significant backend system development but also necessitates ongoing maintenance of internal processes to ensure consistent data categorisation. The additional burden of needing to potentially create ad hoc sub-categories further complicates the process. For platforms operating in specific sectors—such as food delivery or logistics—many of the high-level categories are irrelevant due to the nature of their services and the limited functionality available to users for content generation. A one-size-fits-all approach does not reflect these operational realities.

*Proposal:* Platforms be allowed to exclude high-level categories and associated sub-categories that are demonstrably irrelevant to their business model, user interaction capabilities, or the nature of content disseminated via the platform. This targeted exemption would substantially reduce the administrative burden without compromising the overarching objectives of transparency and accountability.



*Overlapping and Duplicative Obligations with P2B Regulation:* The DSA imposes obligations that partially duplicate requirements already established under the Platform-to-Business (P2B) Regulation, particularly concerning measures taken against business users who breach terms and conditions or disseminate illegal content. This results in parallel reporting duties for similar subject matter, often requiring platforms to build or adapt separate technical infrastructures to meet slightly differing specifications.

*Proposal:* We recommend that the Commission provide clearer guidance and alignment between the DSA and P2B reporting frameworks to avoid redundancy and allow for streamlined compliance across regulations.

*System Adaptability and Transition Periods in relation to DSA reporting:* Adjusting backend systems to accommodate new or amended reporting requirements—especially on short notice—is both technically complex and resource-intensive. The introduction of new data formats or expanded data points necessitates careful re-engineering and testing of compliance systems, which cannot be achieved with short transition periods. In addition to understanding adjustments from a legal perspective, setting up systems accordingly from a technical perspective takes additional time.

*Proposal:* To ensure compliance readiness, any substantial changes to the required data structure or reporting format should be accompanied by a minimum 12-month lead time before entry into force.

*Excessive Retention and Public Disclosure Requirements under the DSA reporting:* The requirement to retain and publicly disclose transparency reports for at least five years imposes an excessive compliance burden with limited practical value. In many cases, the relevance of published data diminishes significantly after 2–3 years, particularly where platform practices or regulatory requirements have evolved. Maintaining public access to outdated data may create confusion or misinterpretation among users and other stakeholders.

*Proposal:* We propose reducing the public retention period to one year, with older reports made available upon request to competent authorities or interested parties. This approach would preserve regulatory oversight while reducing unnecessary storage and publication obligations.

*Mandatory Disclosure of Methodology and Contextual Descriptions under the DSA Reporting*: The templates obligate platforms to provide detailed contextual narratives explaining (i) methodologies for data collection and classification, (ii) contextual background for each indicator (e.g., how decisions were made, how time was measured, why automation was used). These explanations must accompany every reporting point and are often duplicative or immaterial for platforms with low-risk operations or simple moderation models (e.g., logistics apps with limited content interaction). Repeating method descriptions in each cycle offers limited new insight, especially when nothing has changed.

*Proposal:* We propose reducing the public retention period to one year, with older reports made available upon request to competent authorities or interested parties. This approach would preserve regulatory oversight while reducing unnecessary storage and publication obligations.



*Mandatory Classification of Content According to Legal vs. Terms of Service Basis under the DSA reporting:* Platforms must distinguish every action based on whether the action was due to a legal obligation or due to a violation of terms and conditions. Usually Terms and conditions state anyway that illegal content and activities on the platforms are forbidden and that user must comply with all appl This distinction is often difficult to make in practice, especially when legal content overlaps with ToS violations. Preparing two sets of parallel justifications for each takedown introduces risk of error or misclassification.



*Obligations to Report on Precision, Recall, and Accuracy of Automated Systems:* The DSA requires platforms using automated content moderation to report: accuracy, precision, recall and breakdowns by language and input type (e.g. image, video, text). Limit this requirement to Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) or platforms that perform large-scale algorithmic moderation in-house. Exempt platforms that use vendor-based or minimal automation tools.

Could you please confirm me whether we currently have any branded vehicles in Malta? 

On the questions raised, our thoughts are the following:

i) Temporarily suspending a vehicle solely on the basis of it having Uber branding — even if framed around safety concerns — carries a broader risk. We operate hundreds of Bolt-branded vehicles across Europe, and taking steps against competitor-branded vehicles could expose us to reciprocal actions. Branding is a standard commercial practice, and maybe we should be cautious about creating a precedent that could be used against us.

ii) Similarly, limiting operations of these vehicles to specific categories (e.g. Economy) would likely be viewed in the same light. Unless there’s an objective, non-discriminatory reason for such limitations (e.g. clear safety risks supported by rider feedback), maybe we should avoid implementing restrictions that could be interpreted as anti-competitive.

That being said, it might be worth exploring whether vehicle branding for Bolt in Malta is a viable initiative (if we don’t have it yet). Is there interest on your side to consider this?

h3. *For easier understanding: Summary of Information Flow in Bolt’s Admin System*

This diagram illustrates how data flows within the Admin system. Its very high level.

h4. *Step-by-Step Process*

# *Admin User Initiates Action*
The Admin User accesses the *Admin Module* with the intent to view or modify data.
# *User Authentication*
The Admin Module sends the Admin User’s credentials to the *admin-user Backend Service*.
This service validates the credentials using information from the *admin-user database (DB)*.
# *Authentication Info Returned*
The admin-user Backend Service returns authentication details (e.g., user ID, access rights) to the Admin Module.
# *Data/Operation Request Initiated*
The Admin Module then sends a data or operation request (e.g., "show order details", "update account status") to the *admin-user Backend Service*.
# *Backend Coordination Begins*
The admin-user Backend Service forwards this request to additional *Backend Services* (Service 1 and Service 2) that manage relevant business logic or data.
# *Query to Data Stores*
Each Backend Service queries its associated *Data Store* (e.g., Service 1 → Data Store 1; Service 2 → Data Store 2).
# *Data Flows Back*
Results from the data stores flow back through their respective Backend Services → admin-user Backend Service → Admin Module.
# *Response Displayed to Admin User*
Finally, the Admin Module delivers the result (data or confirmation of changes) back to the Admin User.
{panel}

According to this clause, the tax administrator of the Republic of Lithuania has a right to request to disclose certain information from any persons not limiting them to private individuals or other persons whatsoever, if such information is necessary for the performance tax administrator’s functions assigned to it under applicable legal acts.

*Regarding the Acceptance of Option Agreements on the ShareForce Platform*

*Dear Tõnu Kolts,*

In your inquiry, you request our confirmation as to whether the acceptance of options via the equity option management platform ShareForce ([https://www.shareforce.net/|https://www.shareforce.net/|smart-link] ) is sufficient to be considered as a digitally signed option agreement, thereby avoiding the obligation to submit the agreement to the Tax and Customs Board within five working days. *Estonian Tax and Customs Board:*

We confirm that the acceptance of options via the equity option management platform ShareForce is sufficient for the option agreement to be considered digitally signed within the meaning of Section 48, subsection 53 of the Income Tax Act (TuMS). We consider that the acceptance of equity options via ShareForce is in compliance with subsection 53 of Section 48 of the TuMS, as it ensures the reliable identification of the date on which the agreement is concluded.

We explain that the sixth sentence of Section 48, subsection 53 of the Income Tax Act stipulates that if an option agreement is not digitally signed or notarized, the employer is obligated to submit the agreement to the Tax and Customs Board within five working days from the date of conclusion. We clarify that we consider it acceptable if the conclusion date of the option agreement is reliably evidenced by a digital signature timestamp or by acceptance within the employer’s information system where the date is reliably identifiable. As the option acceptance process you have described ensures the reliable identification of the date, there is no obligation to submit the agreement to the tax authority within five working days.

European Commission and European Central Bank gave BG the green light to adopt the euro at the beginning of 2026. Next steps: (1) EU leaders in the European Council will have to approve it by the end of June (26-27 June); (2) the European Parliament is expected to approve an opinion on the draft Council Decision on 8 July; (3) EU finance ministers will then set the exchange rate for converting the Bulgarian currency into the euro on 8 July. Which means BG will have the rest of the year to prepare technically for the transition.

[+An Ordinance amending and supplementing Ordinance No. H-18 of 2006+|https://www.minfin.bg/upload/61436/Naredba+%E2%84%96+N-18++2006.pdf] on registering and reporting sales in retail outlets through fiscal devices, the requirements for software for their management and requirements for persons who make *sales through an electronic store* has been promulgated, according to this [press release|https://evroto.bg/bg/news/219-obnarodvana-e-naredbata-za-izmenenie-i-dopalnenie-na-naredba-n-18-ot-2006-g-#]. 

“The changes are related to the introduction of the euro as the national currency in the Republic of Bulgaria, as well as to the expansion of the functionalities of electronic devices with fiscal memory (…) *the total amount for payment in the issued documents can be displayed in the fiscal receipt in addition to the currency of our country and in another currency*.”

fyi - the Council of Ministers created a mechanism for coordinating monitoring and control and signed a memorandum of cooperation with employers', trade union and industry organisations and associations in connection with consumer protection which will make sure that the process is smooth. Bulgarian National Bank and the Association for Modern Trade (which represents the large retail chains in the country) also signed a memorandum of cooperation.

To build for an iphone:

Go to Xcode, project settings, “Signing & Capabilities”, check “Automatically manage signing”. Create “Personal Team” account.

Then, remove all capabilities that are incompatible with a “personal team” account (use the trash bin icon on the right side).

Make sure you change the Bundle Identifier to something unique (ee.bolt.delierycourier.prelive.<your_name> for example).

You should now be able to build for a device.

!image-20250604-130123.png|width=862,height=364,alt="image-20250604-130123.png"!

On the device, go to settings → vpn & device managament → select you developer app → select trust/verify developer

You should also allow the app to connect to the local network (settings → Local Network).

You can now {{yarn start}} and start the app on the device.

HOWEVER, I had some problems with the iphone being able to connect to the development server while connected to the office wi-fi. The only way I was able to make it work was to connect both devices to a hotspot created on my phone 🙃 

Try also scanning the expo QR code rather than allowing the app to scan for dev server.



Source: [https://github.com/expo/fyi/blob/main/setup-xcode-signing.md|https://github.com/expo/fyi/blob/main/setup-xcode-signing.md|smart-link]

This view is held irrespective of the market share of the supplier/client in question. in practice, applying for an exemption is a lengthy process and not worth the time it take to get it-usually about 6 months and in practice often comes with additional conditions imposed by the Authority e.g as to duration of the exclusivity and scope.

Dear Officer,

We acknowledge your request I-803243, dated 29 April 2025.

Firstly, we wanted to assure you that Bolt understands the seriousness of this request and we look to assist law enforcement whenever we are able to.

At Bolt, we also take the privacy and security of our customers, employees, and independent contractors very seriously. We only engage in data sharing with third parties where we are satisfied that the requirements of our third party data sharing policy have been met. This means that the request for data is lawful, necessary, proportionate, and limited to the specific purpose outlined in the request. 

However, we must respectfully clarify that the structure of the Employer statement form appear to assume a standard employer-employee relationship. This does not reflect the nature of the relationship between Bolt and the individual in question. Bolt connects self-employed independent contractors—such as ABRAHAM RUSSOM—with passengers. These individuals operate as independent service providers and are not employed by Bolt under UK employment law.

For this reason, we are unable to complete the “Employer Statement” portion of the form, as doing so could misrepresent the nature of our relationship and imply an employment status that does not exist.

Nonetheless, we are prepared to provide limited information that we do hold in relation to the individual’s activity on the Bolt platform, in a format that is appropriate to our role as a platform provider. 

We kindly request that you consider an alternative method or format for submitting such data, and we would be happy to discuss this further to ensure compliance and mutual understanding.

Please do not hesitate to contact us should you require further clarification or wish to discuss how we might best support your information needs within the appropriate legal framework.

Yours sincerely,
Bolt

Thanks! The issue with these kinds of “activation fees” is that they may create problems under Apple’s App Store rules. Apple has strict rules: if you charge someone to access an app, that payment usually has to go through Apple’s own IAP system, and they take a 15–30% cut. 

So before we move forward, we need to align with the commerce team on two key points (cc [~accountid:712020:822a759a-daf0-4161-afbf-8b79a2985fba]): 

# *How the activation fee will actually work in practice*
We can’t restrict access to the app based on payment - that would look like a paywall, which Apple doesn’t allow. Merchants must still be able to open and use the app, even if they haven’t paid the €20 fee yet.
# *How we position the fee*
We need to reframe it clearly: this shouldn’t look like a fee for “accessing the app.” Instead, we should describe it as a fee for offline or administrative work - for example, reviewing documents, setting up the merchant profile, uploading menus, or entering business data into the system. The goal is to distance the fee from anything that sounds like app usage or software access.

Investigated the mismatch reasons of total active riders being less than total enrollments (previously found by [~accountid:712020:abc9fd59-ced8-4834-8627-722844558f0d] [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/FPD-777|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/FPD-777|smart-link])  as Priit confirmed it is a suitable approach to follow if we want to get the share of active users enrolled in campaigns. 

*Several reasons for that:* 

# *“Active rider cohorts” should exclude more cohorts - not only churned, not activated, and signups.* We should also exclude everything else except engaged and churning. These are business-defined cohorts, and GA might choose the treatment for them; however, with weekly campaigns, these users will generally not be targeted at all (cherry_picker, corporate_payment, “%ERROR_01”, work_profile).
# *The definition of active rider we use* in {{dev_incentives.weekly_active_riders}}*doesn’t match with lifecycle definitions used by LPCT playbook*. For the input-based model, we defined active riders as those who completed at least one order within the last 90 days. In case of LPCT targeting, the lifecycle stage is determined by the Alive probability model, which uses 12 months of data to get its estimate. As a result, total counts won’t match.
# *LPCT cohorts account for activity in the home city id, while for our calculations* ({{dev_incentives.weekly_active_riders)}}*we account for all cities where user had an order.* For example, there can be a case where the user is active in city A, but their home city is city B. In LPCT definitions, this user might be considered churned, but can still be active according to the definition used by the input-based model. 

An illustrative example of 1 week (2025-03-03) in Paris: 1,344,110 users are ‘active’ based on LPCT cohort targeting  -{{ng_public_spark.etl_incentives_rider_targeting_features}}, engaged and churning cohorts. In {{dev_incentives.weekly_active_riders}}it’s 1,379,328 - *close enough if we exclude all cohorts except churning and engaged but they won’t match 100%.*

h1. Fraud rules for device hard-block

Device hard-block = regardless of the phone number, this device is not able to log in or register an account with Bolt apps. 

*2 types of device hard-blocks:* manually by CS; or automatically via fraud engine.

# Manually via CS when it is confirmed that device was used for criminal activity (fraud, scams, theft, assaults, etc.)

# Automatically via fraud engine only in case of fake rider accounts to create fake orders. These accounts were flagged previously by Fraud team, engine "bulk suspended" them. More infor here: [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C05LLPT628N/p1739273091311619|https://www.google.com/url?q=https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C05LLPT628N/p1739273091311619&sa=D&source=docs&ust=1749125669089003&usg=AOvVaw0PZT2WlxCsVRk7_przN0oE] In the future, Fraud team wants to develop profiling tools to spot fraudulent rider accounts before they cause disruptions.



KB I was referred to: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/360007860954?country=global&language=en|https://www.google.com/url?q=https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/360007860954?country%3Dglobal%26language%3Den&sa=D&source=docs&ust=1749210920147867&usg=AOvVaw3vXVYRLMVx0hfTlke4oCJE] "hard-blocked accounts" - CS (only upon fraud team's instructions) can hard block account and it blocks the device as well. This means that not only will the User not be able to log in to their account, they won't be able to create a new account using the same device. This means that if CS hard-blocked the device this User was using to register / log in, this device must have been connected to Bolt account that was used for fraudulent activity.

Investigated various workarounds for graceful connection draining, the following challenges so far:

* It is complicated to integrate with DB discovery without the risk of discovery disruption or overwriting the state by the discovery process
* With ProxySQL healthcheck implemented in TiDB 8, we need to set up a very long timeout to avoid the host being shunned too quickly (all connections to the host are killed in this case)
* Whatever workaround utilizing graceful-shutdown-wait-time is getting useless

Further investigation did show that most likely we can't use tiproxy (as user-based routing features we need are missing), TiProxy behind ProxySQL won't work either (as ProxySQL is not compatible with connection migration feature of TiProxy).

Most viable option in current conditions seems to be utilizing pre/post scripts and increased delays for restarts handling to allow DB discovery to handle the changes (or override db discovery operations).

Approx sequence is:
PRE:

* make sure no other instances in the cluster are downtimed or wait
* when restart/shutdown is requested, downtime flag is set to instance where script is invoked
* db discovery job is paused (or wait till completion if it's running)
* db discovery json is pulled from S3, updated (host is set to soft_offline), uploaded back
* db discovery is resumed
* wait to allow ProxySQL to fetch new conf
* script is downtime

POST:

* unset downtime flag

{quote}_Dear [_]_

_We regret to inform you that we cannot accept the proposed agreement on the processing of personal data._

_As an online platform, Bolt operates as an independent data controller when serving our business customers. This relationship is consistently governed by Section 4 of our Bolt Business Terms and Conditions, which outlines the conditions under which Bolt and the customer exchange personal data. We do not enter into agreements that alter these established conditions. Our approach and the Terms and Conditions ensure full compliance with GDPR._

_Please note that the notion of controllership in our arrangement is supported by the _[+_EDPB Guidelines 07/2020_+|https://edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-072020-concepts-controller-and-processor-gdpr_en] _on the concepts of controller and processor in the GDPR. _We trust this explanation clarifies our position. Thank you for your understanding._{quote}
----

h3. 1. *Consumer Protection and Fairness*

* *Proportionality and Transparency*: Under EU consumer law (e.g. the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive), any restriction to the service (like locking a user out after failing a test) must be _proportionate_, _clearly communicated_, and not misleading.
* *Terms of Use Update*: Users must be informed in advance through clear T&Cs and/or UI prompts that a sobriety test is mandatory. Failure to do so could result in the clause being deemed unenforceable.
* *Right to Challenge*: Consumers may need a way to challenge or appeal a denied rental if they believe the test was inaccurate or unfair.

----

h3. 2. *Non-Discrimination and Equal Access*

* *Indirect Discrimination Risks*: Tests that rely on motor skills or reaction time could inadvertently disadvantage users with certain disabilities or health conditions, creating risk under the *Equal Treatment Directive* and *national anti-discrimination laws*.
* *Mitigation*: An accessibility assessment and opt-out processes (with alternative verification) may be advisable to avoid unequal treatment claims.

----

h3. 3. *Liability and Risk Allocation*

* *Reliance on Test Results*: If a user passes the test and later causes an alcohol-related incident, Bolt could still face civil liability (e.g. under local traffic laws or civil codes) if the test is shown to be flawed or unreliable.
* *Liability Limitation Strategy*: Use disclaimers and warnings that the test does not replace the user’s legal obligation to be sober under traffic law.

----

h3. 4. *Product Safety and Certification*

* *Medical Device Regulation (MDR)*: If the test involves a physical breathalyzer, it might fall under the EU’s MDR regime, requiring CE certification as a medical device or in-vitro diagnostic (depending on type).
* *Software as a Medical Device (SaMD)*: Cognitive testing apps may also fall under regulatory scrutiny if claimed to detect impairment. In borderline cases, functionality and marketing claims should be narrowly scoped.

----

h3. 5. *Contractual and Operational Considerations*

* *Enforceability of Denial of Service*: National contract law could limit Bolt’s ability to unilaterally block access to services based on test results unless the mechanism is clearly justified, accurately calibrated, and consistently applied.
* *Technical Reliability*: False positives or malfunctions could give rise to user complaints, chargeback disputes, or small claims actions.

----

h3. 6. *National Regulatory Variation*

While EU-wide principles apply, *national laws* (e.g. Germany’s Road Traffic Act, France’s Code de la route) could influence how such a feature is treated, especially if it's seen as bordering on enforcement or surveillance.

Hi [~accountid:712020:05cbf403-315b-4845-a56c-6718f4ea6dbe],

I wanted to share an update on the legal memo (attached) we received from external counsel regarding the *Priority Support Fee (PSF)* in Cyprus.

For context, we requested advice specifically on the local legal implications of introducing the PSF. Leaving aside FinReg considerations, we asked external counsel to advise on the following:

* Whether there are any local laws or regulations that could prevent or restrict the introduction of the fee; and
* Whether there are any additional legal considerations or risks we should be aware of.

In response, external counsel confirmed that there is *no explicit legal restriction* on implementing the PSF under Cypriot law. However, they highlighted a *potential regulatory risk*: even though the fee would be charged by Bolt (and not by the taxi driver), the Road Transport Authority could still interpret it as a supplement to the regulated taxi fare. This is particularly relevant given that, under Law N.9/1982, taxi drivers are only permitted to charge fares that have been approved by the Minister of Transport.

That said, we could argue that the PSF is *a separate, platform-level fee charged directly by Bolt*, not part of the transportation fare. This distinction is key to mitigating the risk of non-compliance.

To minimise this risk, the following *mitigation measures* were recommended:

* Present the PSF as a *separate charge,* not part of the taxi fare.
* Ensure it is *clearly itemised* in the app interface.
* Ensure it *does not affect driver pay* or the regulated fare amount.
* The fee must be *retained by Bolt*, and not passed on to drivers or fleets.
* Clearly link the PSF to *non-transport services* (e.g., business support).
* Maintain full *price transparency* before booking.

The fee definition and the wording proposed for the T&Cs have been endorsed by external counsel.

It’s also worth mentioning that Bolt was previously contacted by the Road Transport Authority in 2025 regarding fare-related issues, so we can assume we may be subject to closer monitoring going forward.

*In summary:* The risk is not zero, but with proper framing and implementation, it can be mitigated. If you and the Ops team are comfortable proceeding with this in mind, I’m aligned from a legal perspective.

Let me know if you'd like to discuss further. 

If you're happy to proceed, please remember that we’ll need to involve the Tax and Billing teams. I'm happy to support you in completing the approval form.

Many thanks!



[^Legal Opinion Legal Opinion- Proposed _Priority Support Fee_ (03_06_2025) (1).pdf]

I have reviewed both the *signed MoU (22/05/2025)* and the referenced *Partnership Agreement (25/07/2023)* between Bolt Operations OÜ and Buzzz Electric Limited. Below is a legal assessment of the client’s change in *Clause 3 of the MoU*, replacing references to an NDA with the 2023 Partnership Agreement.

The *original intent* of Clause 3 in the MoU appears to have been to *govern confidentiality* via a *standard NDA*. However, the *executed version* now reads:

{quote}“The Parties agree that the delivery, receipt and treatment of all information disclosed... shall be governed by the terms of the *Partnership Agreement* entered into... dated 23/07/2023...”{quote}

This *substitutes all references to an NDA with the “Partnership Agreement”*, applying its confidentiality terms to the MoU instead.

After having run a comparative analysis of the confidentiality obligations, I confirm that the 2023 Partnership Agreement includes a full *Confidentiality Clause (Clause 9)* covering:

* Scope of confidential information
* Permitted disclosures
* Duration: *3 years post-termination*
* Purpose limitation and use restrictions
* Carve-outs (public domain, legal requirements, etc.)
* Confidentiality provisions *survive termination* (Clause 12.2)

These provisions are *standard* and similar in purpose and effect to a standalone NDA.

*In conclusion*, the substitution of an NDA with the *Partnership Agreement's confidentiality* +*provisions is acceptable and legally sound*++.+ In fact, the existing agreement offers equivalent or even *stronger protections* than a standalone NDA would.

To recap, +*you can proceed with the signature*+, please let me know if you further need my assistance.

Thanks,

Elisabetta

The Bolt Premium Category booking fee should be subject to the standard VAT rate of 19%. 
There is a reduced VAT rate of 9% for transportation service, but as Bolt is not a transport service provider then it is unlikely that the reduced rate could and should be applied. Further to the legal analysis, the fee is a “separate, platform level fee charged directly by Bolt” meaning that it is not sufficiently linked to the provided transport service, but instead to services of Bolt. The underlying service is related to the mediation of the ride and Bolt’s capacity as an agent.

Subjecting the fee to the reduced VAT rate would go against the nature of the service and increase the risk of the fee being seen as an illegal price increase.

The invoices from driver to business customer should have two lines with different VAT rates.

Due to the fact that this kind of audit can have multiple variables in terms of order of actions/timing/order stats, then in some situations, cancellation fees might not be automatically paid out, however the listed rider accounts should not be penalised for multiple cancellations. * If the driver is close by when ordering (e.g. 1 minute away from pickup location), the auditor should cancel the ride after a delay →  ~2-3 minutes after ordering the ride. _This should not be an issue when the driver ETA is more than 5 minutes._
* If the driver has arrived, and already managed to select “Driving with client“ (start the trip), then the auditor should *not* select “{{not_in_the_car}}“ as the cancellation reason. Instead options like “other“ or “changed my mind“ etc should be selected.


To answer your questions in the commerce-canada-rides thread:

* _If these rider accounts begin to show a high cancellation rate, is there a risk they will be flagged for fraud or blocked?_
While whitelisted, no automatic scheduled blocks or hard-blocks are applied with high cancellation volumes. However, if they still manage to get blocked, feel free to ping me in this ticket or via Slack directly.
* _Will this process negatively impact drivers in any way (e.g., payouts, incentive eligibility, or fraud flags)?_
Drivers will not be impacted via *rider initiated* cancellations, and we don’t flag orders for cancellations. The only down-side for the driver would be the lost amount of work time due to the audit.

If for some reason a driver doesn’t receive the cancellation fee, they should contact CS for a manual compensation.

[~accountid:712020:58fb140c-5d84-43ea-a489-5c7315d1e8b6], as discussed on Slack, could you please review my answer + if you agree with the approach? In short, I think we should decline this request as it concerns a food package (see the picture attached by the reporter), which is not a high value item, and the footage is recorded in the kitchen which is a common area for employees - imo approving the request would have a high risk of creating mistrust among employees and may be potentially harmful for them, as it can create anxiety and affect the overall wellbeing in the office, especially considering RTO and that people are expected to be in the office (which means that they’ll also be having lunch etc there). 

Let me know what you think and if you disagree, we can discuss. Thanks a lot!

----

*Response:* 

Hi [~accountid:5e0f07b262aed90daa48b52d], thank you for your prompt response. Please find my answers to your questions below. 

* *_Isn’t for example, June 12th, 13th, or even the 16th too risky we’ll lose critical data that might undermine our ability to investigate, resolve these cases, and bring this menace to a stop?_*
** You’re right, since the footage would be available until the 16th of June only, we’d do our best to give our approval/disapproval before that date, so there’d be enough time to review the requested footage.
* *_How do we manage the customer’s expectations in the meantime to prevent them from escalating the issue on social media?_*
* *_What if the customer decides to forgo further assistance and take legal action?_*
** While I understand that the customer is dissatisfied and may escalate this in social media / take legal action, granting access to the CCTV footage will not guarantee that the customer won’t escalate this further, as the footage may not reveal who stole the item and/or identifying the person may not solve the issue for the customer. 
** If you need assistance with responding to the customer, please consult with your manager/other relevant teams. If there’s a threat that legal action will be taken, please loop in the Regional Legal team for assistance.
* *_Aren’t some of the employees we’re considering their privacy rights the same people who are behind these theft cases? If they truly valued their privacy, would they be violating company policies in the first place?_*
* *_Aren’t the actions of some of these employees a direct violation of Bolt's policies, warranting investigation and sanctions?_*
* *_How long will this continue—putting innocent employees and our valued customers at risk?_*
* *_Isn’t it time we put an end to this menace once and for all?_*
* *_Conduct a survey of all employees in the office and you will be surprised by the widespread concern about these theft incidents and the strong demand for decisive action. Many are silent not because they don’t care, but because they feel unsupported._*
** While there’s a possibility that the employee behind the theft is on the CCTV footage, there are also other employees who had nothing to do with the situation, whose right to privacy we have to consider. I’d like to highlight again that kitchen is a common area where employees are eating, having informal interactions with colleagues or simply taking a rest, and this would be quite a serious intrusion of their privacy. The kitchen is a common area where employees naturally expect a certain level of privacy and trust. Watching recordings from such area in the office must be extremely well justified. 
** We always assess these situations on a case by case basis. The goal is to carefully assess whether the interest in watching the footage (or the potential risks of not doing so) outweighs the privacy rights of the employee. In this case, the incident involves a missing food package, not a high value item (e.g. a laptop). The interest in reviewing the footage does not outweigh the employees' right to privacy in this case. As this would include watching the footage of a quite long timeframe (I understand it’d be from evening of 26 May until 28 May), and there may be multiple employees in that footage in a shared space like kitchen eating, resting, having private interactions with colleagues etc, approving this request would be disproportionate. While there’s a possibility that an employee/some employees have taken the item, we still have to take into account the fact that there will be employees on the footage that are completely unrelated to this incident, and we need to consider their rights. 

❌ *Due to the above, we will not be able to approve your request. If you have any questions about the reasoning, please let me know.*

Hi [~accountid:5e0f07b262aed90daa48b52d], thank you for your prompt response. Please find my answers to your questions and the outcome below. I’ve also added some suggestions which may help to either avoid or resolve such incidents in the future. 

----

h3. Answers to your questions

* *_Isn’t for example, June 12th, 13th, or even the 16th too risky we’ll lose critical data that might undermine our ability to investigate, resolve these cases, and bring this menace to a stop?_*
** You’re right, since the footage would be available until the 16th of June only, we’d do our best to give our approval/disapproval before that date, so there’d be enough time to review the requested footage.
* *_How do we manage the customer’s expectations in the meantime to prevent them from escalating the issue on social media?_*
* *_What if the customer decides to forgo further assistance and take legal action?_*
** While I understand that the customer is dissatisfied and may escalate this in social media / take legal action, granting access to the CCTV footage will not guarantee that the customer won’t escalate this further, as the footage may not reveal who stole the item and/or identifying the person may not solve the issue for the customer.
** If you need assistance with responding to the customer, please consult with your manager/other relevant teams. If there’s a threat that legal action will be taken, please loop in the Regional Legal team for assistance.
* *_Aren’t some of the employees we’re considering their privacy rights the same people who are behind these theft cases? If they truly valued their privacy, would they be violating company policies in the first place?_*
* *_Aren’t the actions of some of these employees a direct violation of Bolt's policies, warranting investigation and sanctions?_*
* *_How long will this continue—putting innocent employees and our valued customers at risk?_*
* *_Isn’t it time we put an end to this menace once and for all?_*
* *_Conduct a survey of all employees in the office and you will be surprised by the widespread concern about these theft incidents and the strong demand for decisive action. Many are silent not because they don’t care, but because they feel unsupported._*
** While there’s a possibility that the employee behind the theft is on the CCTV footage, there are also other employees who had nothing to do with the situation, whose right to privacy we have to consider. I’d like to highlight again that kitchen is a common area where employees are eating, having informal interactions with colleagues or simply taking a rest, and this would be quite a serious intrusion of their privacy. The kitchen is a common area where employees naturally expect a certain level of privacy and trust. Watching recordings from such area in the office must be extremely well justified.
** We always assess these situations on a case by case basis. The goal is to carefully assess whether the interest in watching the footage (or the potential risks of not doing so) outweighs the privacy rights of the employee. In this case, the incident involves a missing food package, not a high value item (e.g. a laptop). The interest in reviewing the footage does not outweigh the employees' right to privacy in this case. As this would include watching the footage of a quite long timeframe (I understand it’d be from evening of 26 May until 28 May), and there may be multiple employees in that footage in a shared space like kitchen eating, resting, having private interactions with colleagues etc, approving this request would be disproportionate. While there’s a possibility that an employee/some employees have taken the item, we still have to take into account the fact that there will be employees on the footage that are completely unrelated to this incident, and we need to consider their rights.

*Outcome:* ❌  *Due to the above, we will not be able to approve your request. If you have any questions about the reasoning, please let me know.*

----

h3. Suggestions

After discussing this with my colleague, we want to offer some suggestions, given that I understand from your ticket that this is not a one-time situation:

# *Designated internal investigation team:* We recommend forming a dedicated team responsible for internal investigations involving lost or stolen items. Access to CCTV footage should be granted strictly on a *need-to-know basis*, and currently, CS agents are not assigned such responsibilities. Without a clearly authorised role, we would be unable to grant access to CS staff, even in more serious incidents.
## The dedicated team should have the authority to handle such investigations and escalate them to the police if needed. If a request comes from the police, the company can provide evidence directly to support the investigation, as law enforcement has the necessary legal basis and mandate.
## Allowing internal teams without investigative responsibilities to access recordings may be considered unauthorised. Moreover, it's unclear what consequences a person may face if found responsible, which could create legal or ethical concerns. A potential solution is to involve a *neutral party*, such as the People Team, to oversee such cases and ensure decisions are handled appropriately.
## PS. A ticket to the Privacy team would still be required even if such a team is formed, as these cases would still have to be reviewed individually as each case is different. 
# *Designated storage for lost items:* For items left in common areas (e.g. food containers), people might assume they are company-provided — especially if food is normally served in that space. Having a clearly designated and communicated storage area preferably with physical control such as lock for personal or rider items would reduce misunderstandings. If someone were to enter such an area without permission and take an item, that could justify a different approach to footage access, depending on the circumstances.

❗ *PS.* Please note that each case should still be escalated to the Privacy team, this approach shouldn’t be taken with all stolen item cases as they still need approval by the Privacy team and will be assessed case by case.

Let me know if you have any questions.

Eliise

Full data can be found [here|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1WCwoYjMx0a8HmztsR42dtIac11w1qhu8EMb6nwiwOSg/edit?gid=1834930669#gid=1834930669].

Please note this analysis was run on May 29th for the May 21 May – 03 Jun period, so our standard five-day attribution window has not yet completed for the second week.

As a result, additional conversions that occur through Jun 8th will still be attributed to this period.

We will update and share the refreshed numbers early next week once the full conversion window has closed.

This is also supported by the conversions boost when we reran the report for the previous week.

*Pushing to Next Ride:*

* N/A - Shut down.

*Pushing to X Ride:*

* Send-out volumes are up by 56.01%, opens are up by 37.66%, clicks are up by 42.86%.
* Last week’s raw conversions were down -50.00%, but upon re-running the numbers, they are down only by -9.94%, while in the 2 weeks comparison, they are down -8.10%. If last week’s trend continues, we should be seeing an uplift by next week.
* Conversion Rate on track to underperform, due to the spike in Volumes of 56.01%, which needs to be looked into, since we did not change the entry point, only comm cadence.

*High-Value Order:*

Since we don’t have dedicated conversion events for this automations, will focus on engagement metrics:

* Category Upsell - Bolt to Comfort: Continued uptrend with volumes now up from 29.60%  to 32.50% and opens from 28.85% to 45.45%. Open Rates up by 9.78% and Click Rates up by 50.95%.
* Category Upsell - Comfort to Premium: Stabilizing, with increase in send volumes from 21.32% to 52.16% and opens from -20.83% to 9.52%. Open Rates still under previous with a -28.02% drop, while Click Rates are up by 31.44%.
* Category Upsell - Old: Still showcases massive drop across all KPIs. Needs deep-dive to understand which is the main driver. Might be needed to adjust entry point.
* Airport Comms: Still showcases massive drop across all KPIs. Needs deep-dive to understand which is the main driver. Might be needed to adjust entry point.
* Scheduled Rides: Still showcases massive drop across all KPIs. Needs deep-dive to understand which is the main driver. Might be needed to adjust entry point.

*Retention:*

* Continued great performance, with send volume up from last week’s 46.60% to 141.71%, opens up from 114.48% to 201.17% and conversions up by 393.51%.
* Clicks is the only metric which took a hit with a -26.19% drop.
* Conversion Rate up by 104.17%.

*Churn:*

* Send-out volumes are starting to recover. Last week’s -51.90% now is a 2-week -28.74%, which points towards a stabilization & growth in the following weeks.
* but this can also be due to the fact that the old Churn automation has a 25 day journey duration. This means that there are users in the journey from previous week in different steps.
* Enrolment counts for the target 5 markets are stable with 38.93% higher than previous iteration and first e-mail sends are also up by 34.69%, which points towards being on track for higher volumes as well.
* Enrolled vs Sent is also showing signs of stabilization going from -26.54% to -11.89%
* Raw conversions recovered from -65.02% to -25.00% and Conversion Rate is finally in the green with 5.24%. When recalculated, last week’s CVR also went from -27.27% to 37.75%. Therefore we are on track of getting the stats back into the green.

**** if the user was on the list 2 weeks ago, and is still there - do nothing (no row for this user as update not needed)
**** if the user was NOT on the list 2 weeks ago, and is there now (for these 2 reasons) - return TRUE
*** It will be returned in a table (with the first column as external_id), so each iteration will land in the same table, but you will add “compute_date” column is added so only the freshest are taken into account.

:done: This kind of research collaboration can be acceptable from a data protection perspective if certain conditions are met:

* The dataset must be aggregated before it leaves Bolt, with no driver- or vehicle-level identifiers included (even in pseudonymised form).
* The aggregation should be done at a level (e.g. municipality/hour) that ensures no cell reflects the activity of only one or very few drivers.
* The data should be used solely for the described project and not retained or further shared beyond what is necessary for the study.
* Ideally, the dataset preparation should be handled on Bolt’s side to retain control over what is shared.
* The data must not be transferred or accessed from outside the EU/EEA unless appropriate safeguards are in place.

If you can confirm the above holds true, then the sharing should be fine from a data protection point of view.

Hi [~accountid:712020:ae4fba9f-a97d-41eb-8fd7-bec2a5bc17d0] 

I’d consider their Code somewhat stricter than a “standard” code would be.

 E.g.

* _Securitas reserves the right to make periodic information requests of Business Partners, including inspections and/or audits – with or without support of a third party – of facilities, operations and relevant books and records, to substantiate Business Partners’ compliance with the Code. Securitas shall strive to give reasonable notice prior to such information requests. Business Partners are not obliged to disclose information which is subject to confidentiality due to applicable laws and regulations or under contract. Information requests, including inspections and/or audits, shall be subject to proper confidentiality undertakings._ 

Unlikely to happen but ideally we’d not commit to begin with. In the unlikely scenario that it would happen we’d then need to argue and push back on the scope of any inquiry.

* _We must keep accurate records of all matters related to the Business Partner’s business with Securitas. This includes the proper, prompt and complete recording of all expenses and payments and the availability of supporting evidence and documentation._ 

Let’s be mindful not to to mess it up as it’s explicitly stated.

* _Business Partners will accurately reflect any such gifts_ [to Securitas employees]_, meals or entertainment in their books and records._

If that’s in our plans then let’s ensure we record it.

* If a Business Partner fails to comply with the Code, and the non-compliance is not insignificant, Securitas reserves the right to terminate the agreement and business relationship with the Business Partner, *without prejudice to any other rights and remedies available.*

Would be quite relaxed with all the above w/o this bit in bold, i.e. if the only sanction was termination of the main agreement. But the part in bold leaves the door open for further claims - highly theoretical but still. Should we not comply.

Ideally I’d push back on this arguing that termination right should suffice, but not sure how it would be taken or whether the code is actually “take it or leave it”. All things considered I appreciate it might be within our risk appetite to sign it as is.
