As a general principle, the more a platform controls how, when, and whether a driver accepts trips, the more it begins to resemble an employment relationship. If drivers feel compelled to accept every trip to remain online and earn income, this can:

* reinforce the perception that they are economically dependent on the platform; and
* increase their integration into the platform’s core operations - both of which are key indicators of employment status under reclassification tests in Canada.

That said, because drivers would retain full flexibility to go back online and there are no additional penalties attached to being set offline after five consecutive rejections or non-responses, the reclassification risk is moderate - particularly compared to models where offlining is punitive or access is restricted (which would carry a high risk). *The key is that drivers maintain uninterrupted access to the platform and full control over when they work*.

However, it’s critical that this feature is clearly and consistently communicated as a non-disciplinary, operational measure designed to improve rider matching and not as a mechanism to pressure driver behaviour. Even if technically reversible, if not properly explained, drivers may:

* feel compelled to accept trips to avoid being logged off; or
* misunderstand the feature as a form of soft deactivation.

This could undermine the perception of autonomy that supports an independent contractor classification - especially if it influences how drivers behave. Particularly if they are used to the feature on the Uber’s platform where, I believe, there may be negative consequences to the drivers? 

Let’s also ensure we monitor the impact and any driver complaints, particularly if feedback suggests that drivers feel penalised or confused by the feature.

Please feel free to reach out if you have any questions or would like to discuss further.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Information notice*
{panel}

We do not need consent for this processing, but we must inform couriers *at least one week in advance* *via an in-app push notification.* The notice should clearly explain what new data is being collected (three categories you specified), why it's needed, the legal basis we use (privacy side), and how to opt out of such tracking. The proposed draft is below:

_Starting_ *_[DATE]_*_, we will begin collecting additional data from you to help us improve the accuracy of travel time predictions and make deliveries faster and more predictable for clients. This data includes:_

* *_Location metadata:_* _GPS accuracy, bearing, altitude, speed_
* *_Sensors:_* _proximity, light, temperature, humidity_
* *_Network info:_* _connection type (Wi-Fi or cellular), signal strength, and network type (2G/3G/4G/5G)_

_We rely on our legitimate interest to improve user experience by ensuring accurate delivery predictions. Check our_ [_Privacy Notice_|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/privacy-for-couriers/?category=delivery] _for details._

_To opt out, contact CS [LINK] and mention: “I want to opt out of some location data tracking”_ _along with the type of data you'd like to disable._

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Opt-Out process*
{panel}

While it's privacy-preferable (the opt out should happen easy for couriers without a round of CS-Alfred comms) and operationally cleaner to offer in-app permission settings (e.g., a new section in the Courier App showing all tracked location data, their on/off status, and ability to on/off tracking), this requires additional development time. I propose we implement this as *Milestone 2*.

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
For *Milestone 1*, we can begin with a *manual opt-out process*
{panel}

_If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. _Yours sincerely,_

Hi [~accountid:5e65e969c54d0a0d04427b8c] , posting the privacy overview below.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h3. *TL;DR*
{panel}

* :orange_circle: :green_circle: low to medium risk
* *What*: Document rejections are now partly or fully automated using external and internal system outcomes, sometimes involving human review
* *Why*: These decisions can impact driver access to work; if errors occur, drivers may be penalized or frustrated without clear recourse
* *Mitigation*: Strong transparency, clear appeals process, and bias/error monitoring help reduce the risk

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h3. *Key privacy observations*
{panel}

* Even with humans “in the loop,” the system automatically acts on classification logic or error codes. These decisions affect drivers’ ability to work - a sensitive impact that needs careful handling.
* Drivers may not understand why a document was declined, especially if the reason comes from a complex or external signal (e.g. Veritas error). If feedback is unclear, they may keep submitting the wrong document, creating a loop that feels punitive.
* Automatically escalating only after X declines could inadvertently profile certain drivers (e.g. those with poor connectivity or language barriers) and delay their ability to fix the issue.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
h3. *Clarifying questions*
{panel}

* How will the human review look like and how do we define “human in the loop” in this context?
* What is the expected impact on the driver when a document is auto-declined, are they blocked from driving, delayed, or something else?
* What feedback is shown to the driver after an auto-decline? Is it specific (e.g. "document was blurry") or generic?
* What logic determines the X declines before human review? Is it adaptive (e.g. varies by document type)?
* Is there any ongoing QA on Veritas or Beehive outputs that drive declines?
* Is appeal data (e.g. successful reversals) used to improve the system?

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
h3. *Minimal changes to reduce risk*
{panel}

* Show clear, actionable feedback for every decline reason, even if it’s automated
* Trigger human review faster if the same driver is repeatedly misclassified
* Flag escalation thresholds for QA if many declines precede a human reversal
* Surface appeal option visibly and make it easy to use, don’t hide behind CS

h1. 🛡️ Legal Summary: Cyber Security Act 2024 – Implications for Bolt

----

h2. 1. 📘 *What the Act Introduces*

The *Cyber Security Act 2024* is Malaysia’s first dedicated legislation aimed at *protecting national digital infrastructure*. It establishes a *regulatory framework* for managing cyber threats and designates critical systems as *National Critical Information Infrastructure (NCII)*.

h3. 🔑 Key Features Introduced:

* *National Cyber Security Committee (NCSC)*: Chaired by the Prime Minister to set national policies. *That is why the relationship with the cabinet will be crucial.* 
* *Chief Executive of the National Cyber Security Agency (NACSA)*: Granted wide powers to issue directives, demand information, and investigate incidents.
* *NCII entities*: Critical infrastructure operators (public or private) can be formally designated and bound by strict obligations.
* *Providers* of *Cyber Security Service*s will have to be officially licensed. 
* *Incident management framework*: Mandatory notification, audits, enforcement powers, and penalties.

h3. 📌 Covered Sectors (Schedule):

The Act applies to 11 key sectors, including transportation.

h2. 2. 🚦 *Is Bolt Currently Bound by the Act?*

h3. ❌ *Bolt is not automatically bound*

Bolt’s operation in the *“transportation” sector* (a covered sector under the Schedule) does *not automatically* make it an NCII entity. The Act requires *formal designation*.

----

h2. 3. 🏛️ *Designation Process (Section 17)*

The designation process is *discretionary and formalised*, involving the following steps:

h3. 🔹 Who may designate?

* A *Sector Lead* (e.g., Ministry of Transport) may designate *“any Government Entity or person”* (*which includes private companies*).
* The *Chief Executive of NACSA* may also designate a sector lead *as an NCII entity*.

h3. 🔹 Legal Criteria for Designation:

An entity may be designated if it *owns or operates a system*, the *disruption of which would have a detrimental impact* on essential services such as:

* Public safety
* Economy
* National security
* Public order or health

h3. 🔹 Legal Definition of “Person”:

Under Malaysian law, “person” includes:

* Natural persons
* *Companies*
* *Private entities*

⚠️ *Therefore, private sector platforms like Bolt can be designated.*

----

h2. 4. 🔐 *Implications of Being Designated as an NCII Entity*

If Bolt is ever *formally designated*, it would be legally required to implement approved cybersecurity measures, conduct risk assessments and audits, and report any cyber incidents to authorities. It must comply with directives from the National Cyber Security Agency (NACSA), participate in cybersecurity exercises, and provide system-related information on request. Non-compliance may result in fines up to RM 500,000 and imprisonment of up to 10 years. 

h3. 📉 Penalties for Non-Compliance:

* *Fines up to RM 500,000*
* *Imprisonment up to 10 years*
* *Revocation of cyber operations (e.g., service bans or restrictions)*

Why did they refuse to accept our standard terms?

We should *avoid creating a practice* where clients reject our standard T&C, then we offer them to use contract templates that were made for completely different clients.

Those templates are drafted by a specific client, reflect their internal process and still don’t match how our services work. Thus, they’re not suitable for new clients, unless theirs legal team wants to do a good job and critically assess and adjust the template - not the case here.

In this case, I’ll review the agreement for the Central Finance and Contract Agency. But moving forward, we should push clients to use our standard terms even more, explaining the rationale behind (see below):

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
As a rule of thumb, +we do not work with client-provided templates+. If this practice has been followed previously, it needs to be changed due to the inconsistencies, additional risks, and obligations we undertake by signing clients' agreements.

+*Supporting arguments for this practice:*+

# Bolt Business General T&C are specifically tailored to Bolt's business model, services, and platform. Client's templates are not suitable for Bolt's business model and require heavy adjustments, which is a time-consuming process for both parties, making it neither effective nor rational.
# Using the service provider's template is standard business practice. It is the most rational and streamlined approach, saving time for both parties, as only the service provider fully understands their product and drafts documents to reflect its specifics. Even the largest credit institutions in the Baltics use Bolt's standard template.

*If a client resists:* If a client insists on using their template, we can communicate our strict internal policy: if the contract value is below EUR XX (the business can set the exact amount), we do not accept client templates because the resources required for review are disproportionate to the contract value. If a client still prefers their template, they should increase the contract value. This approach will not only save time for our sales and legal teams on low-value contracts but may also motivate clients to increase the deal value.
{panel}

Hi [~accountid:5b7be9e6b8e3cb589585eb47] and thank you. Posting my summary/findings below.

*Summary:* This case concerns a single unauthorized ride taken on a rider account (User A) where the rider alleged suspicious activity. Upon investigation, the issue appears attributable to recycled phone number reuse rather than credential compromise or system breach.

----

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h3. Findings
{panel}

# *Cause: Recycled phone number*
#* Both User A and a newly created account (User B) were linked to the same phone number.
#* Device and account were both created on 4 March 2025 — strongly indicating that the phone number had been reassigned by the telecom provider, and Bolt’s systems subsequently linked it to a new rider.
#* No evidence suggests account credentials or OTPs were shared or intercepted.
# *Scope and impact:*
#* One unauthorized ride was taken by the new account holder (User B) before the issue was discovered.
#* There is no indication of broader access to User A’s historical account data, nor were any sensitive fields (name, email, payment card, etc.) reported as modified.
#* User A’s account was subsequently deleted on 13 April 2025, per their request.
# *Mitigation steps taken:*
#* All devices were logged out as an immediate precaution.
#* User A’s account was deactivated and later deleted.
#* Issue flagged with broader regional visibility (Spain) for ongoing trend monitoring.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h3. Privacy Risk Assessment
{panel}

* *Data exposure risk:* Low. No evidence that the new user accessed historical personal data tied to User A. Visibility was likely restricted to default post-login UI content before deletion.
* *Legal exposure:* Minimal. The root cause was telecom recycling, not Bolt system error or breach. Timely mitigation and user communication occurred.
* *Reputational/user trust risk:* Localized, limited to the affected individual. No cluster of similar cases reported at this time.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h3. Resolution
{panel}

* ✅ User A’s account is fully deleted.
* ✅ No remaining data appears linked to the recycled number.
* ✅ Incident is contained and not ongoing.

No further action is required at this stage. Logging and closing the incident with this case recorded.

Understood. I’ll investigate the legal obligations in Denmark regarding in-vehicle camera use for taxis and ride-hailing services. This includes the applicable provisions of taxi law, the scope of their application (e.g. whether they apply to ride-hailing platforms), data storage and retention requirements, signage and transparency duties, and broader GDPR compliance aspects. I’ll get back to you with a clear and structured memo.

h1. *Memo: Internal Camera Use in Danish Taxis and Ride-Hailing Vehicles*

h2. *1. Mandatory In-Vehicle Cameras for Taxis and Ride-Hailing Services*

*Legal Obligation:* Danish taxi legislation imposes a clear obligation to equip taxis with interior video surveillance. Under the Taxilov (Taxi Act) effective 1 January 2018, _“vehicles used for taxi service must be fitted with interior camera surveillance”_. This requirement was introduced alongside other safety measures (e.g. taximeters and seat sensors) as part of a nationwide taxi reform. Notably, there is *no general exemption* – it is legal to use CCTV in taxis and, in fact, now mandatory in Denmark. (Earlier rules had allowed local councils to exempt taxis doing primarily contract/pre-booked work from the camera mandate, but the current unified taxi law does not appear to provide such broad exemptions.)

*Scope – Traditional Taxis vs. Ride-Hailing:* The camera mandate applies to *all vehicles operating “taxi driving” services*, which by law includes rides booked through a licensed dispatch platform (a _kørselskontor_). In practice, this means both traditional taxi companies *and* drivers on ride-hailing platforms like Bolt must comply. The law expressly requires that any car providing taxi rides sold via a dispatch service be equipped with a taximeter, seat occupancy sensors, and an interior camera. Therefore, a ride-hailing vehicle in Denmark is treated the same as a taxi for regulatory purposes if it carries paying passengers.

*Responsible Parties:* The obligation to install and maintain the camera primarily falls on the taxi permit holder or vehicle owner (e.g. a taxi company or independent driver) as part of the vehicle requirements. However, *Bolt’s dispatch center role* means it must ensure that all affiliated drivers’ vehicles meet these legal equipment standards. Bolt cannot legally dispatch rides to non-compliant vehicles without risking violation of taxi regulations. In summary, the Danish law effectively makes in-car cameras a _condition of operating_ a taxi or app-based ride service – covering the full spectrum from traditional cab fleets to ride-hailing drivers – rather than a voluntary security option.

h2. *2. Collection, Recording, and Storage of Camera Footage*

*Purpose Limitation:* The use of in-vehicle CCTV is intended _exclusively for security and crime-prevention_. Legislative materials emphasize that recordings should be handled appropriately and _“only disclosed to the police for criminal investigation purposes”_. In other words, the footage is collected as evidence or deterrence against offenses (e.g. assaults, robberies) and not for any arbitrary use. Taxi companies or drivers are generally not to use or share the recordings beyond what is necessary for safety, incident resolution, or law enforcement.

*Storage and Retention:* Danish law and guidance impose strict limits on how long CCTV recordings may be kept. Under the TV-overvågningsloven (CCTV Act), video recordings made for crime-preventive purposes *must be deleted no later than 30 days after recording* (unless needed longer due to a specific ongoing investigation or dispute). This “30-day rule” is a legal requirement to ensure data is not stored indefinitely. There is _no requirement_ to keep footage for the full 30 days if not needed; in practice many systems automatically overwrite or purge data after a shorter period unless an incident has been flagged. Importantly, if a particular recording is *likely to be used as evidence (e.g. a reported crime or formal complaint)*, it may be retained beyond 30 days _for that purpose_, but routine retention beyond 30 days without cause is not allowed. Taxi operators should therefore have procedures to automatically erase footage after the standard retention period, barring any exceptional need to preserve it for police or legal proceedings.

*Security Measures:* All footage collected must be stored securely. While Danish law does not prescribe specific technologies, it implies that camera systems should produce usable, high-quality images and safeguard them from unauthorized access. In practical terms, this means using approved camera systems (often encrypted and tamper-resistant devices installed in the vehicle) and restricting access to the recordings. Typically, only designated personnel (e.g. a company security officer) or law enforcement can unlock or download the footage. Bolt and its partner fleets should ensure that any recorded data is protected (through technical and organizational measures like encryption, access logs, etc.) in compliance with GDPR security requirements. They should also implement clear procedures for handling footage (who may retrieve it, how it’s transferred to authorities, etc.), consistent with data minimization and purpose limitation principles.

*Location of Storage:* Danish rules do not explicitly dictate where the footage must be stored (onboard vs. cloud), but the common practice is for the *camera system to store video locally in the vehicle* unless an incident triggers a need for retrieval. This local storage approach limits continuous data transfer and access. Bolt should verify that drivers use camera systems that meet any police or regulatory specifications – for example, cameras rugged enough for vehicle use and capable of capturing identifiable images. The National Police have authority to issue guidelines or orders regarding CCTV quality and storage for private operators, so any such guidelines (e.g. resolution standards or secure storage requirements) should be adhered to. Overall, Bolt should treat the camera footage as highly sensitive personal data: collected only for safety, stored briefly and securely, and accessed strictly when necessary.

h2. *3. Transparency and Passenger Notification Obligations*

*In-Vehicle Signage:* Danish law mandates transparency whenever CCTV monitors areas accessible to the public or serves as workplace surveillance. Under the TV-overvågningsloven, *any private entity monitoring a place with public access (or a workplace) must inform people by clear signage or notice*. A taxi is both a workplace (for the driver) and a space open to passengers, so this rule squarely applies. Thus, taxis *must display a visible sign inside the vehicle* to notify passengers that video surveillance is in operation. Earlier taxi-specific regulations explicitly required _“visible signage in the vehicle’s cabin informing about the CCTV”_, and this aligns with the general law’s requirements. In practice, Danish taxis commonly have stickers or placards (often pictograms of a camera and text) in the passenger compartment. Bolt should ensure drivers affix the prescribed notice in each car so that riders are aware of the camera from the moment they enter.

*Content of Notice:* The signage should at minimum indicate that surveillance is taking place. While the law doesn’t dictate exact wording, best practice under GDPR’s transparency principle is to include who is operating the cameras and for what purpose. For example, a sign might state: “*CCTV in operation for security*.” Some taxi companies also provide a contact (or link to a privacy policy) for more information. Danish Data Protection Authority guidance notes that the GDPR *“oplysningspligt”* (duty to inform data subjects) applies alongside the basic sign – meaning additional information about the data processing should be available upon request or via an online privacy notice. Bolt, as a dispatch service, should incorporate information about in-car cameras in its privacy policy and possibly in the app/website, explaining the purpose of recording, retention period (30 days or less), and contact details, to supplement the on-site notice in vehicles.

*Passenger Consent:* Notably, passengers do *not* need to give consent to be recorded in the taxi – surveillance is authorized by law and justified by safety interests. The signage and privacy notice serve to inform rather than seek permission. However, transparency is crucial for building trust. Bolt may consider advising users (e.g. via app notification or FAQ) that rides in Denmark are subject to CCTV for safety, which is a legal requirement. This level of openness can help preempt customer concerns.

In summary, clear and prominent *in-vehicle signage* is required by law, and Bolt should also ensure that riders can easily access further details about the camera surveillance and their rights (for instance, by referencing Bolt’s privacy policy or the taxi company’s contact on the signage).

h2. *4. Data Subject Rights and Law Enforcement Exemptions*

*Right of Access to Footage:* Under GDPR, individuals (passengers or drivers captured on the in-car video) have the right to request access to their personal data, including video recordings. In principle, a passenger can submit a subject access request to see footage that contains them. Danish practice, guided by the Data Protection Authority, allows controllers to fulfill such requests in a limited and safe manner. Specifically, the controller *should only provide images of the requesting person and not reveal other individuals in the video*. This often means extracting still frames or short segments where the person appears, with other passengers or the driver *blurred or redacted* for privacy. If blurring others is impossible (for example, in a tightly confined shot), the controller may decline to release those portions to avoid violating others’ privacy. The Danish DPA has indicated that supplying a series of *still images* can generally satisfy an access request – there is _no obligation to hand over the entire video or any audio_ if still frames adequately show the person’s data.

In practice, a rider who wants to see camera footage of a trip would likely need to contact the taxi company or Bolt’s data protection contact. Bolt should have a process to coordinate such requests (since the data may be stored with the driver or vehicle unit). As a controller, Bolt cannot simply refuse an access request, but it must balance it with the privacy of others and safety considerations. It’s worth noting that frivolous or extremely broad requests can be narrowed (the individual only has right to *their* personal data on the footage).

*Right to Erasure and Retention Limits:* GDPR’s right to erasure (“right to be forgotten”) may be invoked by a subject, but in the context of CCTV, there are important caveats. First, as noted, *routine deletion will occur after 30 days* for all footage by default. If a passenger requests deletion of a recording in which no incident occurred, chances are the data will auto-delete within the legal timeframe anyway. Controllers are allowed to reject an erasure request if keeping the data is necessary for certain reasons – for instance, *establishment or defense of legal claims* (GDPR Art. 17(3)(e)). In a taxi context, this means if the footage is needed as evidence for an ongoing dispute, accident, or crime, it will not be erased even if an individual requests it, as it serves a legitimate legal purpose.

*Exemptions for Investigations:* When footage is retained for *law enforcement or security reasons*, data subject rights can be curtailed. Danish law (the Data Protection Act and CCTV rules) provides that the 30-day deletion requirement does _not_ apply if a recording is being used in an active police investigation (in such cases, the data can be kept as long as needed for the case). Similarly, if a passenger who was recorded committing an offense were to request access or deletion, the controller could lawfully refuse during the investigation. GDPR Article 23 allows Member States to restrict rights like access and erasure to safeguard the investigation of criminal offenses. Denmark’s implementation indeed permits withholding or delaying disclosure of CCTV images to avoid tipping off offenders or compromising evidence. Once a recording has been handed over to the *police*, it falls under law enforcement data rules, and the individual would then have to follow procedures under those rules (which typically limit access until proceedings are finished).

*Practical Handling:* Bolt should be prepared to handle data subject requests jointly with its taxi partners. For example, if a rider asks Bolt for “any camera footage of my ride on X date,” Bolt as a dispatch/controller should liaise with the relevant driver or fleet that holds the footage. Any response must ensure *no personal data of others is improperly revealed*. Bolt should also train that footage needed for safety or legal matters is exempt from deletion until resolved. All such requests and responses should be documented in accordance with GDPR accountability. In summary, *data subjects can exercise their rights*, but with significant limitations: they are only entitled to their own image/data (often provided as still photos), and crucially, if the footage is needed for an incident report or law enforcement, the request can be lawfully refused or deferred.

h2. *5. Bolt’s Responsibilities and GDPR Compliance Considerations*

*Role as Data Controller:* In its role as a licensed _kørselskontor_ (dispatch platform), Bolt bears legal responsibilities for compliance regarding any personal data processed in the course of its services – this extends to camera data when used. While individual drivers or taxi permit holders physically install and operate the cameras, Bolt will likely be considered at least a *joint data controller* for footage insofar as it is used to fulfill Bolt’s services (e.g. handling safety incidents or passenger complaints). Indeed, the taxi law obliges dispatch centers to have a customer complaint system and join a Taxi Complaint Board. In investigating complaints or safety issues, Bolt may need to obtain and review video recordings from a vehicle. For example, Bolt’s Danish privacy notice should (mirroring industry practice) disclose that camera recordings from vehicles *may be processed in complaint handling or safety investigations*. Thus, Bolt cannot distance itself from the camera data – it must ensure that its operational policies cover this processing.

*GDPR Legal Basis:* Bolt should confirm the lawful basis for processing in-car video. Since installing cameras is a *statutory requirement*, processing the footage to comply with that law and to ensure safety can be based on *GDPR Article 6(1)(c) (legal obligation)*. The Taxi Act essentially obliges having surveillance, which provides a strong ground. In addition, *legitimate interests* (Article 6(1)(f)) in protecting drivers and passengers can supplement this basis – Danish authorities have viewed crime prevention in taxis as a legitimate interest, provided privacy safeguards are in place. Bolt should document its assessment of these bases in its GDPR records. If any footage might incidentally capture special categories of data (for instance, revealing health condition or racial/ethnic origin of a passenger), an additional justification (such as if needed for establishment of legal claims, Art. 9(2)(f)) would apply, though generally the video is standard personal data.

*Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA):* The use of continuous interior cameras in vehicles carrying the public is likely considered a high-risk processing activity (it involves systematic monitoring of potentially vulnerable individuals in a confined space). GDPR requires a *Data Protection Impact Assessment* for surveillance activities in public areas or large-scale monitoring. Bolt should either conduct its own DPIA or ensure one has been done in the context of its service. The DPIA should evaluate the necessity and proportionality of the camera surveillance, the risks to individuals’ privacy, and the safeguards in place. Given that the measure is mandated by law and aimed at safety, the DPIA’s focus would be on ensuring proper restriction of access, secure storage, timely deletion, and transparency. If Bolt is onboarding many drivers, it should verify that each has an approved camera system and possibly maintain a record (inventory) of these cameras, including confirming they are registered with the police if required (note: as of March 2021, Danish law requires that fixed cameras covering public spaces be registered in the national POLCAM database; interior taxi cams may not squarely fall under “cameras in areas of ordinary traffic,” but Bolt should clarify if any registration is expected).

*Operational Policies and Training:* Bolt should implement clear policies for drivers regarding the cameras. This includes rules that *drivers must not tamper with or disable the cameras during operation*, and that they must follow protocol if an incident occurs (for instance, secure the footage and notify Bolt and police). Misuse of camera footage by a driver (such as downloading and sharing clips of passengers) would violate GDPR and Danish law – Bolt needs to communicate that such misuse is prohibited and could lead to termination and legal consequences. From a GDPR standpoint, drivers could be seen as Bolt’s agents or independent controllers; either way, Bolt should contractually bind them to handle the video data lawfully and only for the intended purposes. It may be prudent for Bolt to offer guidance or tools for drivers on how to handle data access requests or police inquiries, so that these are routed properly through Bolt’s compliance team.

*Additional Risks:* Bolt should be aware of the following compliance risks and requirements:

* *Security Breaches:* If camera footage is leaked, hacked, or lost, it would constitute a personal data breach. Bolt would likely need to report serious breaches to the Datatilsynet (Danish DPA) within 72 hours and possibly notify affected individuals, especially given the sensitive nature of video (imagine footage of a passenger altercation being posted online – this would be highly damaging). Preventive measures like strong encryption on storage media and strict access control can mitigate this risk.
* *Data Minimization:* The cameras should not record more than necessary. They generally cover the interior of the car; there is no audio in many systems (some jurisdictions disallow audio to reduce intrusiveness – Denmark’s rules focus on video). Bolt should avoid any expansion of camera use beyond security (e.g. not use it for driver monitoring beyond what’s legally required, unless that has been assessed separately).
* *Transparency & Consent:* As discussed, explicit consent is not the basis here (legal obligation is), so Bolt must be careful to fulfill transparency requirements in lieu of consent. All riders should be informed, and drivers too should be informed of the surveillance in their workplace. Bolt’s privacy policy and driver agreements must reflect the presence of CCTV and how data is handled.
* *Cooperation with Authorities:* The law expects taxi camera data to be available to police for crime investigation. Bolt should have a point of contact to handle police requests or warrants for footage. Providing footage to law enforcement *is permitted and expected* in crime cases; this transfer is allowed under GDPR as necessary for compliance with legal obligations or for legitimate interests in crime prevention. Bolt should ensure any handover to police is documented (what was given and under what authority) and that no footage is given out to anyone else (no third-party disclosures except the Taxi Complaint Board or similar oversight bodies, as required).

In conclusion, *Bolt, as a dispatch platform in Denmark, shares responsibility for ensuring that in-car cameras are implemented and managed in full compliance with Danish law and GDPR*. There is a legal obligation to have these cameras in all vehicles it dispatches, and with that comes the duty to handle the footage properly – including secure storage (max 30 days), clear signage for passengers, respect for individuals’ rights (access to their own images), and cooperation with law enforcement when needed. Bolt should incorporate these requirements into its operational protocols and privacy compliance program. By doing so, Bolt not only fulfills its legal responsibilities but also helps protect passengers and drivers, fostering trust in the safety of the service.

*Sources:*

* Taxilov (Law No. 1538 of 19 Dec 2017, as amended): §25(4) requiring taxis to have interior cameras.
* Summary of new Taxi law (Danish Transport Authority) – requirement of taximeter, seat sensors, and camera for all taxi services via dispatch.
* Danish Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) guidance on CCTV: signage duties and 30-day deletion rule.
* Dansk Erhverv (Danish Industry) advisory on fulfilling access requests for surveillance footage with still images.
* Dantaxi Privacy Policy (example of industry practice) – use of taxi camera footage for handling complaints and 30-day default retention.
* Legislative history (Folketinget) on taxi CCTV – purpose limited to security and police access.

I checked the % of unique scooters that have had at least one short ride a day. 

[^Oslo_30days short rides (3e19bab7-eb45-4e17-af5d-5dd33cdbb88f).xlsx]

Weekly data shows that the % of unique scooters within short orders is dropping, this shows that the % of short rides is rising because certain broken vehicles are collecting bad feedback. 

!image-20250609-154245.png|width=1307,height=682,alt="image-20250609-154245.png"!

So far we have identified that scooters are collecting bad feedback and short rides in Oslo for following reasons: 

# Suspicious rides criteria of 5/5 orders which are less than 150 meters and less than 60 seconds is too restricting. We have seen many scooters where scooter gets more than 5 continuous rides less than 100 meters, but atleast one of them is longer than 60 seconds. This essentially “resets” the suspicious ride counter, meaning that now it has to get another 5 short rides which are less than 60 seconds. 

!image-20250609-163909.png|width=659,height=498,alt="image-20250609-163909.png"!
## This could be fixed by either increasing the time criteria or changing the amount of previous rides checked for suspicious orders. 
# Currently in Oslo, a scooter will get a bad user feedback collection task if 5/5 feedbacks have been negative. The set criteria is very restricting, because if one of the orders gets a feedback which isn’t “bad” ( meaning that it’s not brakes_problem, tire_problem, does_not_start or needs_repair) then the feedback counter essential resets and will be waiting for the next 5 orders with “bad” feedback.
## This could be fixed by changing the collection task marker criteria to 3/5 user bad feedback, like it is in most Dragon cities. 

h3. Repeat offenders

So far I have checked 12 scooter that had the collected the most short rides. 

I checked that for 7/12 of these scooters, the problems started before firmware update. 4/12 scooters problems started after multiple successful rides with new firmware. There was one scooter where the problems could have started right after the firmware update. 

1/12 scooters had an error E261. It was not collected because error E261 was set to level 4 in IoT error collections. It was set to level 4 because of Cobra ECU firmware bug that was discovered a year ago. Now that the Cobra ECU firmware bug is fixed, [~accountid:5e9a112618b8ed0c0f776390] changed E261 error collection to level 1 {{2025-06-09}} .

1/12 scooters had a problem with brakes. It could be seen from telemetry that the brakes were applied from the beginning of most orders. 

!image-20250609-163615.png|width=988,height=577,alt="image-20250609-163615.png"!

1/12 scooters had a problem with throttle. It could be seen from telemetry that throttle was applied right at the beginning of an order for all orders. In the logs it could also been seen that WECU was reporting E256 - throttle error. For some reason this error didn’t create a collection task for the scooter. [~accountid:5e9a112618b8ed0c0f776390] sent the order log to [~accountid:6220bd4194f7e20069fe8306] for analysis. 

!image-20250609-163632.png|width=987,height=575,alt="image-20250609-163632.png"!



3/12 scooters had an issue with wheel speed. From telemetry data it could be seen that wheel speed stayed zero or had negative spikes, when GPS speed acted as expected. For example, from GPS graph it could be seen that scooter is pushed above 5 km/h, but wheel speed stayed 0. Telemetry also shows that throttle was pushed and brakes were not applied. 

!image-20250609-163538.png|width=1000,height=582,alt="image-20250609-163538.png"!

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt and Neste (oil refining and marketing company) are entering into a cooperation agreement. Concerns loyalty program for Bolt drivers. Plan is to launch at start of June.
** Between local Bolt Latvian entity and Neste Latvian entity.
** Under the agreement, both parties will cooperate in promoting a Neste loyalty program for fuel and convenience to Bolt drivers. Neste will then provide Bolt drivers with a discount.
*** Neste will issue pre-activated payment cards with set discounts. Discounts are for diesel and gasoline.
*** Bolt responsible for “_Contacting the Drivers registered on the Bolt platform to encourage them to use Loyalty Program by giving out Neste payment cards with set discounts to drivers. Bolt shall use Bolt Driver App, Bolt Blog etc. and other internal communication channels… Specific details of the Loyalty Program (discounts) shall be listed in the communications to drivers_”.
*** Bolt shall also “provide information about the Loyalty status of each Driver once a month”, at which point Neste shall update the driver’s loyalty status info. Unclear exactly what this info is.
** Seems to be based on Neste standard form.
* Clause 8 deals with data protection. States that both parties must comply with data protection laws and ensure lawful basis. Otherwise repeats Appendix B.
* Appendix B deals with data sharing. Appears to be loosely based around Bolt standard form.
** Specifies that parties are ICs.
** Data to be shared: 
*** Bolt → Neste: Phone number, email address and loyalty status.
*** Neste → Bolt: Driver’s loyalty status update, and data of overall transactions made by Neste payment cards (sounds aggregated).
** Clause 9 states “In the sign-up process, Bolt will ask the driver’s consent to share personal data with [Neste]” - this is not correct.
** Clause 12 states the parties shall ensure their privacy notices are compliant - no point in having this in (and in any case, could bite us without PN updates).

Hi [~accountid:62a7061fbf7afc006f3a8000] - thanks for your patience. I have reviewed a local copy of the agreement and my thoughts are below. In short, there are two key privacy issues here: (1) reviewing the provisions of the data sharing agreement; and (2) privacy issues relating to Bolt marketing Neste’s discount to Bolt drivers.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*(1) Review of agreement*
{panel}

I have included my comments on the agreement / Appendix B in a local copy here ([+*LINK*+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1udlLCx6Q6JRVq8Z9p8s_LuWSmoQDKLCP/edit]). My edits primarily focus on Appendix B (the data sharing agreement).

It looks like various provisions from Appendix B were lifted directly from out standard form - is this correct? (i.e., {color:#ff5630}*Who originally drafted Appendix B - us or Neste?*{color}) Assuming that we originally prepared Appendix B, it is quicker / more efficient / more protective of Bolt’s position to just use our standard form rather than go through each provision - I have therefore taken this approach, and updated the standard form with the relevant details. I have also removed the provision that previously said Bolt would obtain driver consent before sharing their data with Neste -  we should not be signing up to this obligation for the reasons set out in my comment bubbles in the document.

The only {color:#ff5630}*action items from your side*{color} are as follows:

* Review Appendix B, fill out the sections highlighted in yellow (e.g., date), and confirm that you do not have any concerns.
* Answer the questions highlighted in comment bubbles - in particular, presumably we are not sharing any data outside of the EU / with any other third parties under this agreement?

In an ideal world, we would get our Information Security Team to review Neste’s IS compliance measures, although I assume there will not be time for this. If this is correct, the redrafted provisions will at least mitigate some risk here.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*(2) Bolt marketing Neste’s discount to Bolt drivers*
{panel}

I understand that under the collaboration agreement, Bolt will be communicating Neste’s discount drivers. Depending on how Bolt sends these communications to drivers, the communications may be caught by direct marketing rules. {color:#ff5630}*Could you therefore please confirm how Bolt intends to do this*{color}?

* If we plan on notifying drivers about the discount in a way that is *_not targeted to specific drivers_* (e.g., via in-app banners or via a general page on the platform), then this is unlikely to be caught by direct marketing rules and this is fine from a privacy POV.
* If we plan on notifying drivers about the discount in a way that is *_targeted to specific drivers_* (e.g., via push notifications, emails or SMS), this is likely to be caught by direct marketing rules. In this case, we can only send the communications to users who have opted-in to receiving them (i.e., by consenting to receiving ‘Partner Offers’), and such users must have an easy way of opting-out of such communications. Primary Investigation of the Incident:

h2. 🧾 Summary of Current Findings: OTP Fraud in Ghana - More to be found in the Report linked below.

h3. 1. *Incident Overview*

* *Fraud Type*: Targeting *riders* (mainly *business clients*) through *WhatsApp impersonation* of Bolt CS agents.
* *Objective of Fraudsters*: Gain access to high-credit-limit accounts, place high-value orders (especially through Bolt Food), and extract value through early cash-outs or resellable goods.
* *Scope*:
** At least *20 rider accounts* affected (2 excel sheets to be found in the report).
** Total *estimated financial loss*: GHS 82,992.08 (still confirming the details).
** *3 accounts deleted*. 

h3. 2. *Fraud Mechanics*

* *OTP harvesting via WhatsApp*, often through impersonation using Bolt branding.
* *Passkeys* and *social media integration* used to retain persistent access.
* Device or account deletion sometimes used to evade detection or recovery.

h3. 3. *Bolt's Current Response*

* Accounts compromised are logged out; passkeys disabled.
* Some devices could not be removed due to social logins.
* *Partial refunds* issued in only 4 cases. In general, we are *avoiding refunds.*

----

h3. ✅ A. *Incident Management & Operations*

Under Maltese law, vehicles with more than eight passenger seats—such as minibuses with nine or more seats—do *not* fall under the scope of the _Light Passenger Transport Services and Vehicle Hire Services Regulations_ (Subsidiary Legislation 499.68). 

Minibuses fall under the _Passenger Transport Services Regulations_ (S.L. 499.56), which govern the operation of passenger transport vehicles for hire or reward with more than eight passenger seats. Operators of such vehicles are required to obtain a *Carriage of Passengers Operator Licence (CPOL)* issued by Transport Malta .

Hi team, 

The payment failed with an error message 82 : Negative CAM, dCVV, iCVV, CVV, or CAVV results. 



The error message *“82: Negative CAM, dCVV, iCVV, CVV, or CAVV results”* typically means that the card security check failed during payment authorization.

# *CAM, dCVV, iCVV, CVV, CAVV*
These are various types of *card verification values*:
#* *CVV / iCVV*: Card Verification Value (used in magnetic stripe and chip cards).
#* *dCVV*: Dynamic CVV (used in EMV / chip cards).
#* *CAM*: Card Authentication Method (for validating the card in EMV chip transactions).
#* *CAVV*: Cardholder Authentication Verification Value (for 3D Secure / online transactions).
# *Why does it happen?*
#* The CVV or security code entered is *incorrect*.
#* The card is potentially *compromised* (fraud detection measure).
#* *Expired or damaged card*.

*What to do?*

* Double-check the CVV and try again.
* Ensure that you entered the security code correctly.
* If the issue persists, contact the *issuing bank* for further help.


Cheers, 
Marten

h2. ✅ Key Legal Considerations Confirmed

h3. 1. *Risk-Based Security Deposits*

* *Legitimacy*: Applying higher deposits to drivers based on risk profiles (e.g. age or rental timing) is a standard and justifiable commercial practice. It is commonly used in the car rental industry to offset the risk of accidents or misuse.
* *Transparency*: You mentioned that the criteria are _transparently communicated_ in the Bolt App. This is crucial for both *contract law* compliance and to mitigate any *consumer protection* concerns.

h3. 2. *Non-Discrimination*

* Differentiating based on *age* or *rental timing* is generally permissible if grounded in legitimate risk factors and *not arbitrary*.
* Make sure the criteria do not inadvertently lead to indirect discrimination (e.g. if a certain age group correlates heavily with another protected characteristic). Based on your description, this does not appear to be an issue.

h3. 3. *Data Protection and Privacy*

* You noted that _privacy safeguards are in place_. This is essential, especially if driving data, behavioral patterns, or age are being processed to assess risk.
* Ensure:
** Lawful basis for processing (likely performance of contract or legitimate interest)
** Data minimization (only what's needed for deposit logic)
** Transparency in the Bolt App’s privacy notice

----

h2. ⚠️ Potential Additional Considerations

h3. 1. *Unfair Contract Terms (EU Consumer Law)*

* *Clear Presentation*: The terms around deposits must be _clearly and prominently displayed_ before the user confirms the booking.
* *Proportionality*: The deposit amounts must be *reasonable and proportionate* to the potential risk or damage. Excessive deposits could be challenged under unfair terms legislation.

h3. 2. *Regulatory Trends or Country-Specific Nuances*

* While this approach is broadly acceptable across the EU, *local consumer agencies* or *national interpretations* might vary slightly. For example:
** In Germany, consumer protection regulators have historically scrutinized automated decision-making or profiling related to pricing or security deposits.
** France and the Netherlands also tend to be more protective of younger consumers.

h3. 3. *Right to Explanation / Profiling Concerns*

* If your deposit calculation is automated and significantly affects users (e.g., access or pricing), *Article 22 GDPR* may apply. Based on your description, the deposits are additive rather than determinative, so the impact may not meet the “significant” threshold—but it’s worth monitoring.

----

h2. ✅ Conclusion

Yes, your understanding is largely correct: this practice is *low risk*, *aligned with industry standards*, and legally defensible—*assuming*:

* Full transparency
* Reasonable and proportionate deposit amounts
* Robust data protection controls
* Regular review for fairness and accuracy

h2. ⚖️ LEGAL ASSESSMENT OF NEW RISK FACTORS FOR SECURITY DEPOSITS

h3. 1. *Driver’s Licence Issued Outside the Rental Country*

h4. ✅ Legal Basis

* *Legitimate risk rationale*: Licences issued outside the rental country (especially from non-EU jurisdictions) may correlate with differing driving standards, lack of reciprocal enforcement, or less predictable driving records.
* *Permitted differentiation*: It is generally permissible to treat drivers differently based on the *country of licence issuance*, particularly if grounded in risk mitigation.

h4. ⚠️ Legal Risks

* *Potential indirect discrimination*: Differentiating based on licence origin could indirectly affect nationality or ethnic groups, especially if licences from specific countries are disproportionately impacted.
* *Country-specific scrutiny*: Consumer protection authorities in some EU countries (e.g. DE, NL, FR) may question whether the risk data justifies the differential treatment.

h4. 🔧 Mitigation

* Ensure *objective and verifiable risk data* supports the differentiation (e.g. claim rates or accident rates by licence origin).
* Make sure this criterion is *applied consistently* and proportionately.
* Avoid overgeneralising (e.g., not all non-EU licences represent higher risk).

----

h3. 2. *Use of Residence Permit as an ID (vs. EU/EEA ID or Passport)*

h4. ⚠️ High Sensitivity Area

h4. Legal Considerations

* *Risk of indirect discrimination*: This factor may correlate strongly with *nationality*, *migration status*, or *ethnic origin*, making it vulnerable to legal challenges under:
** EU Equality Directives
** National anti-discrimination laws
* *Questionable link to driving risk*: Unlike licence origin, the use of a residence permit *does not inherently relate to driving ability or responsibility*.

h4. 🔧 Recommendation

* *Do not use this criterion* unless you have *robust empirical evidence* linking it to increased risk (e.g., significantly higher claim or incident rates).
* Consider whether *ride history or licence origin* already captures the intended risk differentiation more appropriately.

----

h3. 3. *Ride History (Frequency and Tenure)*

h4. ✅ Low Legal Risk

h4. Legal Considerations

* *Established risk proxy*: Recency, frequency, and length of engagement are widely used in fintech and mobility to assess user familiarity, loyalty, or predictability.
* *Permitted under consumer law*: Provided this is applied *transparently*, the practice is unlikely to breach EU legal standards.

h4. 🔧 Safeguards

* Ensure thresholds (e.g. what counts as “frequent”) are reasonable and clearly communicated.
* Provide *user recourse or exceptions* (e.g. users new to Bolt but experienced drivers).

----

h3. 4. *History of Speeding Warnings or Driving Bans*

h4. ✅ Strongest Justification

h4. Legal Considerations

* *Directly linked to safety risk*: Use of objective, prior violations is standard and legally defensible.
* *No discrimination risk* if based solely on documented driving behaviour.

h4. 🔧 Implementation Tips

* Define clear parameters (e.g. how long a warning is relevant—6 months? 12 months?).
* Offer a clear user notice or explanation if a higher deposit is required based on this criterion.

----

h2. 🔍 GENERAL IMPLEMENTATION CHECKLIST

||Risk Factor||Legal Justification||Legal Risk||Recommendation||
|Licence Origin|Medium–Strong|Medium|Proceed with caution and justification|
|Residence Permit as ID|Weak|High|Avoid or delay; seek stronger justification|
|Ride History|Strong|Low|Safe to proceed|
|Speeding History|Very Strong|Low|Safe to proceed|

----

h2. ✅ FINAL RECOMMENDATIONS

* *Avoid including migration status or residence permits* unless absolutely necessary and supported by data.
* *Document your risk logic* for each trigger and review it periodically (e.g. every 6–12 months).
* *Ensure transparency*: Each trigger must be clearly explained in the Bolt App to avoid claims of unfair or opaque contract terms.
* *Offer a redress mechanism*: Consider enabling users to contest a high deposit, particularly where the trigger is not based on driving history (e.g. licence origin).

Hello [~accountid:712020:233144b7-8984-4e6b-922e-2ed0d6700d5f]! Here is the output of the query for May: [^Bolt_Plus_Comments.csv]. 

The [*notebook*|https://bolt-common.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/558923859719846?o=3598988355446810#command/7008389888925657] is in Databricks, and I wasn’t able to find your email when trying to share the notebook. 



However, here is the Databricks query separately as well (it needs to be run on pii cluster for access to {{sel_customer_support_pii_spark.support_case_comments_v2}}):

{code:sql}-- all unique cases with user comments that include 'bolt plus' or 'bolt +' in May 2025
with comments as (
  select 
    distinct support_case_id,
    date_format(created_date, 'yyyy-MM') as created_month
  from sel_customer_support_pii_spark.support_case_comments_v2
  where 
    created_date between date('2025-05-01') and date('2025-05-31')
    and user_type != 'admin_user'
    and (
      lower(comment) like('%bolt plus%') 
      or lower(comment) like('%bolt +%')
      ) 
)

-- final query with aggregation
select 
  c.created_month,
  fsc.support_case_vertical,
  fsc.support_case_user_persona,
  count(c.support_case_id) as count_support_cases
from comments c
inner join core_models_spark.fact_support_case fsc
  on c.support_case_id = fsc.support_case_id
where fsc.support_case_state not in ('draft','duplicate')
  and fsc.is_incoming_support_case
  and fsc.support_case_created_date_utc > date('2025-01-01') --partition the fact_support_case table, so it doesn't scan entire table
group by 1,2,3
order by count_support_cases desc
limit 100{code}

h3. Investigation 

All three BMS ( SN’s ) share the same symptoms. 

I removed the U1 LDO and applied 3.3V from an external power supply. Power consumption was 190mA at 3.3V, in normal conditions it should be 10 mA. Checking the BMS with a thermal camera showed that the MCU is the first component that heats up when power is applied. MCU is also the only component that heats up to 60°C. 

It is possible to connect to the MCU with a flasher and it’s possible to flash the MCU, but flashing didn’t change anything, power consumption was still 190mA 3.3V. 

-I checked that RS485 doesn’t have power because VCC3 line is 0V. MCU should enable this power, but for some reason it’s not doing that. VCC3_EN is 0V.-  VCC3 was 0V, because ID pin was not pulled to GND. If ID pulled to GND, then VCC3 is the same as VCC2.

_Hey team, we've discussed the benefits topic again among_ [_@anton.diatlov_|https://taxify.slack.com/team/UNG39C4H1]_,_ [_@thomas.wagner_|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U06PRA349NE]_,_ [_@kamaljeet.dhiman_|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U043969T4JE]_,_ [_@rose.cooperfinger_|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U07H1P2G5PS]_,_[_@aleksandr.ivanov_|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U05AM2HE04D]_,_ [_@pedro.araujo_|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U066W2PDU1X]_, and_ [_@pavel.nekrasov_|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U01G3ATPT0V]_, and here is our consensus:Since we still have low confidence on:_

# _How scoring would affect user behavior_
# _How scoring would affect damage rates and costs_
# _How user scores would fluctuate between rides (e.g. user gains benefit on one day then loses it on the next)_
# _How much users will complain about their score accuracy (CS tickets, etc.), especially in the case of disputes regarding hard benefits,_

_It hence makes most sense to launch first without benefits (A/B partial rollout) to see how users would react to the scoring visibility alone. In terms of user sentiment, we would not have any new incentives or penalties initially, so it shouldn't be that serious of an effect on engagement. However, we would still communicate to users that "benefits are coming soon" to encourage them to improve their score in preparation for a benefit becoming available._

_Then, in Q3, we would introduce the first benefit, and then rollout the feature to the entire user base. We would then have higher certainty on benefit choice and expectation of how it would affect P&L, and we would have measured the impact of each lever/change in isolation._

+*Update:*+ 

* We have been informed that as part of proceedings initiated by Lime against Liverpool Council (“the *Council*”), Lime is now seeking disclosure of confidential information, including potentially Bolt’s *overhead cost data*.
* A *specific disclosure hearing is scheduled for 13 June 2025*, and Lime continues to seek inclusion of one of its senior employees (Mr Raccagna, Government Affairs Director) in the *confidentiality ring,* a legal mechanism allowing access to sensitive materials.
* We attended a meeting with the Council on Wednesday 4 June (notes from meeting set out below).  
* We prepared a witness statement (attached to this ticket) which was filed by the Council on Friday 6 June. 

+*Notes from meeting on 4 June (which was sent to the business in slack)*+

*_Summary of the Current Position and Today’s Discussion Points_*

# _The Council is currently in the process of preparing a witness statement from their side, which will emphasise Bolt’s concerns about disclosing commercially sensitive information to a competitor._

# *_Bolt confirmed the following:_*

* _Although we are broadly comfortable with the existing confidentiality protections in the draft order, we reiterated our concern about the extension of the confidentiality ring to Mr Raccagna._
* _We raised questions about how enforceable the confidentiality ring would be in practice (i.e. if Mr Raccagna were to breach the terms of the confidentiality ring, it would be difficult to prove this in practice). Note that, although the Council acknowledged this point, the focus of the call was on sharing sensitive financial information (summarised below)._
* _Although we are comfortable with disclosing mobilisation costs and total overheads, we reiterated that we are_ *_not_* _comfortable with sharing how that figure was achieved (i.e. the breakdown of such costs), and that information should be redacted._

# *_The following was agreed between Bolt and the Council:_*

* _The Council will try and have a discussion with Lime’s legal team and ask whether the Council can share information that redacts profit share and overheads, with the aim that Lime will have clarity around the fees (and ultimately see that they were not “abnormally high”)._ 
* _There is a possibility that, upon receiving the redacted information, Lime’s legal team requests further information and argues that we need to disclose more (which the court may agree with on the basis that it may be material). However, neither party knows at this stage what the court’s approach will be._
* _If Lime’s legal team persist, Bolt will prepare a witness statement stating the reasons why this information should not be shared, the impact of sharing such information etc._

*_The Council’s Strategy_*

* _Although the Council has considered abandoning the tender and re-running it, having received external counsel, they do not want to go down this route at this stage for the following reasons:_
** _it will result in delays, especially as the trial expires in March/May 2026; and_
** _it would be difficult to re-run the tender process and do it fairly. This is because all bidders have received feedback on how their bid has done against Bolt’s bid, and if the tender was to be re-run, it would mean that each bidder would have an advantage which would render the whole process unfair._
* _The Council’s procurement team has undertaken a review and is confident that the process was run properly and compliantly._
* _The Council’s strategy, at present, is to apply to lift the suspension and make the contract award to Bolt._

*_Agreed Next Steps_*

* _The Council will contact Lime’s legal team regarding possible narrowing of disclosure, and will provide us with an update._
* _The Council will send us a framework of what is needed for Bolt’s witness statement. Once received, we will take a view on whether we will prepare a witness statement or attend the hearing on 13 June._[^Witness Statement_Bolt Operations UK Limited_Lime Technology Limited_Liverpool City Council_06.06.25.pdf] 

+*Next Steps:*+

* We are currently waiting for advice from external counsel on whether we should attend the hearing on Friday 13 June (in any capacity) and the costs associated.

*Investigation/Explanation*

*Storing chargeback notification*

Chargeback defence process starts with incoming chargeback notification from PSP. Fraud gets those notifications from Payments via MQ.

Fraud listens to notifications here: 

[https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/b36cd0c2280fd41a5f172e7c1f40600af639e7ac/src/platform/commerce/fraud_data/main/payment_data/service/chargeback_notification/ChargebackNotificationSyncService.ts#L59|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/b36cd0c2280fd41a5f172e7c1f40600af639e7ac/src/platform/commerce/fraud_data/main/payment_data/service/chargeback_notification/ChargebackNotificationSyncService.ts#L59] 

During introduction of SilverFlow, raw json notification payload was removed from MQ events.

Due to limited time (we didn’t allocate dedicated time to support SF project, because we had other projects in priority), we did only minimally required changes. So, notification payload became {{""}}
See this code and comment: 
[https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/b36cd0c2280fd41a5f172e7c1f40600af639e7ac/src/platform/commerce/fraud_data/main/payment_data/service/chargeback_notification/ChargebackNotificationSyncService.ts#L234-L244|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/b36cd0c2280fd41a5f172e7c1f40600af639e7ac/src/platform/commerce/fraud_data/main/payment_data/service/chargeback_notification/ChargebackNotificationSyncService.ts#L234-L244] 

*Processing chargeback notification*

The 1st step of preparing chargeback dispute document is to collect required data. Required data is collected by a set of loaders.
Loaders are declared in {{RidesDataCollector}} and {{DeliveryDataCollector}}
There is {{PaymentNotificationLoader}} which loads chargeback notification data and tries to parse raw json payload.
See here: [https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/33ae484b4aad2a54a9a25deb2ca06fc48e47cecc/src/platform/commerce/fraud_chargeback_dispute/main/chargeback-dispute/service/document_creator/data_loader/PaymentNotificationLoader.ts#L61|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/33ae484b4aad2a54a9a25deb2ca06fc48e47cecc/src/platform/commerce/fraud_chargeback_dispute/main/chargeback-dispute/service/document_creator/data_loader/PaymentNotificationLoader.ts#L61] 

It can’t parse {{""}} JSON, thus an error is logged. 

All errors are caught and process continues. However, following data fields are not available anymore for dispute documents:

* authorisation data - what was authorized during original payment operation
** {{amount}}
** {{authorization_code}}
** {{currency}}
* chargeback amount - what was requested to chargeback

So, some sections in chargeback dispute documents are missing



*Required fix*

* remove raw payload parsing

Find below the list of remaining principal issues which need internal business/risk decision (which to accept, where to continue pushing back) and then alignment with EY respectively. _I’ve also cleaned up the_ [_agreement draft_ |https://docs.google.com/document/d/1O0_oyEJz3wG3s8IAyBCYwg_yGCpo81XZnC9-cYkuFdg/edit?tab=t.0]_as far as possible accepting all what can be considered harmless enough for us, but I wouldn’t share that externally until the below has been taken into account for drafting purposes._

❗ When deciding on the below be mindful about the long term of the agreement (3+1+1 years) and the extremely narrow rights we have to terminate the agreement termination (section 10).

# *Liability for driver partners* (c. 9.2). I’m not aware of any single customer globally with whom we have accepted such liability (as we are a platform operator). Bare in mind we have already suggested c. 2.7 regarding our commitments towards driver partner’s compliance (already a stretch). *Would require MGMT/ Reclass. Risk Committee approval.*
# *Insurance* (c. 7). Likely we don’t have what EY is asking (“as bare minimum”). *Requires gap analysis with Insurance, or some risk taking should acquiring the relevant coverage not deemed viable/optimal.*
# *Liability* *overall* (section 9). 

* EY insists on broad exclusions from limitations for various heads of liability (confidentiality, data protection, IP indemnity, anti-corruption).
* Mutual cap of £500,000 accepted, also exclusion of consequential loss, but carve-outs effectively nullify the cap for key risks.

*Advise to:* 

* accept carve-out for liability that cannot be excluded under applicable law and for IP and anti-bribery indemnity, but ideally push back on confidentiality and data protection (appreciate might not be viable so if the we get the below two points in then could be acceptable);
* push to exclude consequential losses entirely (except where non-excludable by law) without further carve-outs.
* Confirm mutual cap of £500,000 applies to all other losses.

# *SLA’s* (appendix 2). While my understanding is that you’ve aligned with Rides Ops operationally then as for remedies per EY this shouldn’t be limited to just the “Resolution” column but section 9 (see above point 3) should apply. *Advise to push back on this.* 
# *Supplier Code of Conduct* (13.9). Should be within our risk appetite to accept it as is if the sole remedy was EY’s right to terminate the agreement. But they pushed back on this. Could be in our risk appetite to nevertheless accept it if we manage to agree on a somewhat reasonable liability section (see point 3 above).
# *Monthly Billing* (c. 13.8.2). We explained how monthly billing would require subscribing to a different offering (Business account) which they seemed to understand however in this clause they still aim to get us to commit to enabling billing fast-track somehow. *Advise to additionally explain the specifics of how our products work.*
#  *The rebate* (appendix 1). I’ve cleaned it up as it was super messy but still some comments remaining so not clear if final and approved commercially by both parties.
# *Notice of Change of Control* (6.3); *Assignment* (c 13.6); *Anti Corruption* (c. 11). We are fine with respective commitments ourselves but merely asked to make this mutual, they refused w/o meaningful argument. Wouldn’t consider this a deal-breaker (difficult to foresee a scenario where it might materially harm us) but always alarming if counterparty is not ready to have such elementary things on par which is why ideally we’d push back but.
# Bolt’s ability to claim against EY is *limited to entity for whom the service is rendered* + EY wants *all network entities to be third-party beneficiaries with right to enforce against Bolt* & EY’s right to submit claims itself should a network entity not do so for some reason. (c 3.16) Again, should be on par, but possibly we’re forced to accept.

Check Competition Authority annual reports from 2019 to date available at [https://cak.go.ke/planning/annual-reports|https://cak.go.ke/planning/annual-reports|smart-link]- in those reports, they publish summaries of the decisions they have made on various issues or advisory opinions they have given. Narrow down to the decisions/opinions on restrictive trade practices in the context of exclusivity as a guide to see their view on the issue. Some summaries:

h2. Legal Implications of Exclusive Agreements & Restrictive Trade Practices

h3. 1. *Violation of Sections 21 and 25 of the Competition Act*

* *Section 21* prohibits restrictive trade practices, including:
** Price fixing
** Market allocation
** Agreements that significantly lessen or prevent competition (including exclusivity clauses without approval).
* *Section 25* allows exemption applications for restrictive agreements *only if* they demonstrate overriding public interest or efficiency gains.
* *Legal implication*: Entering into exclusive agreements without CAK approval constitutes a violation of Section 21 unless exempted under Section 25.

h3. 2. *Hard-Core Restrictions Are Non-Negotiable*

* Clauses such as *price fixing* and *resale price maintenance* are considered *hard-core restrictions*.
* *Legal implication*: They are *not eligible for exemption* unless compelling public interest is demonstrated — a very high bar.

h3. 3. *Non-compliance with CAK Orders*

* Companies failing to comply with CAK directives (e.g., to expunge exclusivity clauses) may face:
** *Enforcement actions*
** *Fines and penalties*
** *Cease-and-desist orders*
* *Legal implication*: These actions serve as deterrence and signal the Authority's willingness to escalate enforcement if directives are not followed.

h3. 4. *Public Interest & Market Impact Are Key*

* CAK weighs exclusivity’s *impact on market access*, *consumer choice*, and *price levels*.
* *Legal implication*: Exclusivity can only be allowed where benefits clearly outweigh anti-competitive effects.

----

h2. 📊 Table: Fines/Sanctions Related to Exclusive Agreements & Restrictive Trade Practices

||*Year*||*Parties Involved*||*Nature of Agreement*||*Legal Basis*||*Outcome* / *Sanction*||*Citation*||

|2020/21|*Koko Networks & Vivo Energy*|Territorial exclusivity and price setting|Sections 25 & 26|*Price-fixing clause rejected*; exclusivity granted for 5 years. Non-compliance detected, later resolved after *compliance checks*| |
|2020/21|*Billerudkorsnas AB* (complaint by Cugini Paper Traders)|Alleged product exclusivity|Sections 21 & 24|*No action* – no exclusivity found or dominance established| |
|2023/24|*Windson Chemical Pvt Ltd*|Sought 10-year exclusivity in formaldehyde production|Section 25|*Exemption denied* – did not meet statutory thresholds| |
|2023/24|*KQ & Precision Air*|Exclusive JV clauses|Section 25|*Exemption granted* for 6 years| |
|2018/19|*Cooper K-Brands & Partners*|Product exclusivity, territorial limits, resale price maintenance|Sections 25 & 26|*Exemption granted* only for product exclusivity; other restrictions *rejected*| |

The  proposed increase in the suggested (estimated) fare displayed to passengers in Athens could be legally permissible, provided that the disclaimer and pricing model remain aligned with the following core regulatory principles:

# *The Suggested Price Can Be Indicative*
 According to Greek consumer and transport regulation, platforms *are not required to display a fixed price* upfront as long as:
#* The estimate is clearly labeled as such, and
#* The method of final price calculation (i.e., taximeter-based) is clearly communicated.
 The disclaimer you’re currently using *meets these conditions*. It explicitly states that the fare shown is _informational_, may vary, and the final price is set by the taximeter.
# *Final Price Must Reflect Taximeter Calculation*
 Under _Ministerial Decision No. 191290/2022_, taxis in Greece must calculate trip costs via *taximeter*, and this final amount is *what drivers are legally required to charge*.
 Since the *platform is not replacing or modifying the taximeter fare*, but merely providing a higher pre-trip _estimate_, this remains compliant.
# *You ensure* that the updated higher estimate still *reflects a plausible upper-bound* price based on historical ride data. While it can be conservative, it must not be misleading.

* *You* continue to *display the full disclaimer clearly* before booking confirmation. It helps reinforce transparency and protects Bolt from complaints or liability.
* If a portion of the fare increase relates to the platform fee (rather than meter fare inflation), it should remain clearly *labeled in app and on the self-billed invoice.*

To recap, your plan to increase the *suggested fare estimate* for Athens is *legally sound*, under the following conditions:

* The *taximeter remains the sole determinant* of the final fare.
* The *driver issues the receipt*, not Bolt.
* The *disclaimer continues to clarify the fare is estimated* and subject to change based on distance, time, etc.

I have carefully reviewed the DLA memo and my understanding is that under *Ministerial Decision 191290/2022*, taxi fares in Greece are *strictly regulated* and calculated using a taximeter. 

The memo clearly states that under *Greek Law 4530/2018*, a platform becomes a *regulated transportation service provider* if:

* It *grants unlawful discounts or subsidies on fares*, or
* It *determines the amount to be paid by the consumer by other means*.

A *€5 coupon*, even indirectly applied, *may be interpreted as such a discount* if publicly communicated and used to offset a fare.

h4. *Sanctions for Non-Compliance*

* *Fines* between €10,000 and €50,000.
* *Revocation of platform license* after repeated violations.
* *Immediate €50,000 fine* if operating without a platform operator license while promoting prices.

The proposed messaging carries a *significant legal risk* under Greek ride-hailing laws if:

* The benefit is *perceived as a discount* on a regulated fare;
* It is *publicly advertised* by influencers.

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*In short:*

* It appears that in Poland we can ask for a photo of a passenger’s ID to verify their gender in the context of W4W.
* However, we should not +*store*+ the full copy of the passenger’s ID - we do not have a strong legal basis to do so under Polish law. Instead, we should extract the gender field, and then delete the photo of the ID.
* If the user objects to the processing, we can: (i) delete the gender field retained (but flag that the user would need to re-verify); (ii) explain that we do not retain the copy of the ID and only refer to the gender field; and (iii) flag that the user is free to use other features.

[~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd] nothing for you to action here - I have just done a deep dive into this topic and wanted to record my findings somewhere, so this is just an FYI in case you ever need to refer to it.

----

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*(1) Is collecting copies of passenger ID an offence under Polish law?*
{panel}

In short, although a grey area, it is {color:#36b37e}*unlikely*{color} that Bolt would be caught out here. (/) 

* The Polish Act on Public Documents prohibits collecting and storing “_replicas of public documents_” without an explicit legal basis for doing so (this is separate to aGDPR legal basis), due to risks of forgery. This offence carries criminal liability.
* The definition of a ‘replica of a public document’ is a copy of a public document (e.g., passport or ID) possessing “_features of authenticity_” - secondary research shows photocopies or scans of such documents are unlikely to count as they would not include “_optically variable paint, elements visible under UV light or other elements that ensure the security of an identity card_”. Logically, this also applies to photos taken on a passenger’s phone.
* As such, collecting and storing a *_photo_* of a passenger’s ID does not appear to be explicitly an offence under local Polish law, given that it does not have features of authenticity and in any event is not collected and used in a forgery context. Local counsel confirmed this position separately.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*(2) Are there any legal issues with storing copies of passenger ID in this context?*
{panel}

In short, {color:#ff5630}*yes*{color} - We should not be storing the full copy of the ID. ❌ 

* Even though Bolt is unlikely to be caught by the Polish Act on Public Documents, the GDPR will still bite here, particularly with regards to data minimisation, storage limitation etc. It would be easy to argue that the full photo of the ID is not needed - only the gender field (particularly re indefinite storage).
* Polish UODO has repeatedly cautioned against collecting full ID scans without strong necessity (_"In the regulator’s opinion, making copies is permitted only when the law explicitly authorizes one to do so._”)
* Based on previously discussions with Ernesto and Sara, the main reason we are retaining full copies of the ID is so that the passenger does not have to provide it again the next time they want to use the category. This is likely now redundant in light of the gender field check that has been introduced (particularly as, per previous advice to the business, gender field should be stored separately). Ernesto is fine with deleting the ID photos, but the verification tam / Veritas handles this.
* As such, to not be caught out under the GDPR, we should (unless we have a strong reason for doing otherwise): *(i) ask for the photo of the ID; (ii) immediately extract the gender field (which we can retain); and (iii) proceed to delete the photo of the ID from our systems*. An auto-deletion solution would be preferable - This would substantially mitigate the risks here.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*NEXT STEPS*
{panel}

*(a) Advice to Safety / Verification Teams*

* Do not advise PESEL alternative - this is even higher risk..
* Veritas owns the system for deleting IDs. We should ask for auto-deletion feature once the gender field has been extracted, where docs are collected in the context of W4W. This has been requested [+*here*+|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C090VCL558U/p1749576033873709].
* Also worth checking whether an appeals process was actually implemented for users that feel excluded from the category.

*(b) DSAR response strategy*

* Rely on legitimate interest as a legal basis (does not appear to be contractual necessity, as not strictly necessary / not explicitly in T&Cs / etc.), but avoid conflating this with legal basis under Polish Act on Public Documents.
* Emphasise to rider that their ID is collected to extract the gender field, and their ID is otherwise stored with storage limitation principles in mind. Avoid going into further details for now until auto-deletion is implemented. Reiterate that users can object to data processing.
* Flag to rider that the category is voluntary - if they do not want to provide their ID, then can use other categories.

*(c) Internal documents*

* I note that we previously concluded a LIA / DPIA was not needed. In light of the Polish context, we should consider revisiting this.
